fresnel-equations-reflection-refraction.title: Fresnel Equations, Brewster's Angle and Total Internal Reflection
fresnel-equations-reflection-refraction.content:
When harmonic Monochromatic Plane Waves strike a planar interface separating two homogeneous, linear, nonmagnetic dielectrics of refractive indices n1 and n2, source-free Maxwell's Equations enforce strict continuity of the tangential electric field E∥ and tangential magnetic field H∥ across the plane. Satisfying these Boundary Conditions everywhere along the boundary requires incident, reflected, and transmitted waves to share an identical tangential wavevector component, immediately establishing specular reflection (θr = θi) and Snell's law of refraction \( n_1 \sin\theta_i = n_2 \sin\theta_t \). Because electromagnetic Transverse Fields decouple into orthogonal s-polarized (transverse electric, TE, with E perpendicular to the incidence plane) and p-polarized (transverse magnetic, TM, with E parallel to the plane) states, matching tangential amplitudes yields the exact Fresnel reflection coefficients \( r_s = \frac{n_1 \cos\theta_i - n_2 \cos\theta_t}{n_1 \cos\theta_i + n_2 \cos\theta_t} \) and \( r_p = \frac{n_2 \cos\theta_i - n_1 \cos\theta_t}{n_2 \cos\theta_i + n_1 \cos\theta_t} \), with transmission amplitudes ts = 1 + rs and tp = (n1/n2)(1 + rp).

At normal incidence (θi = θt = 0), where s- and p-orientations coincide, both \( r_s = \frac{n_1 \cos\theta_i - n_2 \cos\theta_t}{n_1 \cos\theta_i + n_2 \cos\theta_t} \) and \( r_p = \frac{n_2 \cos\theta_i - n_1 \cos\theta_t}{n_2 \cos\theta_i + n_1 \cos\theta_t} \) reduce in magnitude to |(n1 − n2)/(n1 + n2)|, predicting 4.0 percent power reflectance at an air-to-crown-glass (n2 = 1.50) surface and a π-radian phase flip upon external reflection from a denser medium (n2 > n1), while grazing incidence (θi → 90°) drives reflectance toward unity for every dielectric. Quantifying optical power transport requires projecting the time-averaged Poynting Vector onto the interface normal; because refraction alters both wave impedance (1/n) and beam cross-sectional width (cosθ), normal energy-flux conservation across a lossless boundary takes the form \( R = |r|^2, \quad T = \frac{n_2 \cos\theta_t}{n_1 \cos\theta_i} |t|^2 = 1 - R \). This impedance-matched flux partitioning closely parallels reflection and mode conversion of longitudinal and shear waves at solid boundaries in Linear Elasticity, Stress-Strain and Waves.

Inspecting the numerator of \( r_p = \frac{n_2 \cos\theta_i - n_1 \cos\theta_t}{n_2 \cos\theta_i + n_1 \cos\theta_t} \) exposes a sharp asymmetry between polarizations: whereas rs remains nonzero for all angles whenever n1 ≠ n2, p-polarized reflection vanishes identically when n2 cosθi = n1 cosθt. Combining this null condition with \( n_1 \sin\theta_i = n_2 \sin\theta_t \) forces reflected and refracted rays to stand strictly perpendicular (θi + θt = π/2), fixing Brewster's polarizing angle \( \tan\theta_B = \frac{n_2}{n_1} \)—roughly 56.3° for air-to-crown-glass (n2 = 1.50) and 53.1° for air-to-water (n2 = 1.333). Physically, the refracted electric field drives bound molecular dipoles perpendicular to the transmitted wavevector; at θB, those dipoles oscillate directly along the specular reflection axis, and because an oscillating electric dipole radiates zero power along its own axis, no p-polarized wave scatters back into medium 1. Unpolarized light reflecting near θB thus acquires pure s-Polarization, enabling glare-suppressing sunglasses and zero-loss Brewster windows inside gas lasers, whereas absorbing metals with complex indices exhibit only a nonzero pseudo-Brewster minimum.

Reversing propagation from an optically denser medium into a rarer medium (n1 > n2) introduces a qualitative threshold in \( n_1 \sin\theta_i = n_2 \sin\theta_t \). Above the critical angle θc—41.8° for crown glass into air and 24.4° for diamond (n1 = 2.42) into air—sinθt exceeds unity and cosθt turns purely imaginary. Substituting imaginary cosθt into \( r_s = \frac{n_1 \cos\theta_i - n_2 \cos\theta_t}{n_1 \cos\theta_i + n_2 \cos\theta_t} \) and \( r_p = \frac{n_2 \cos\theta_i - n_1 \cos\theta_t}{n_2 \cos\theta_i + n_1 \cos\theta_t} \) yields unimodular complex amplitudes (|rs| = |rp| = 1), enforcing total internal reflection with unit reflectance and zero net normal energy flow. Yet tangential continuity sustains a non-propagating evanescent wave inside medium 2 gliding along the surface while decaying exponentially with normal depth z as exp(−κz) over sub-wavelength distances, governed by \( \sin\theta_c = \frac{n_2}{n_1}, \quad \kappa = k_0 \sqrt{n_1^2 \sin^2\theta_i - n_2^2} \). Rapid angular variation of reflection phases φs and φp above θc imparts a lateral Goos–Hänchen displacement to finite beams, while the differential phase φp − φs powers achromatic Fresnel-rhomb retarders.

Bringing a second high-index dielectric prism within a sub-wavelength gap d comparable to the evanescent decay length 1/κ of \( \sin\theta_c = \frac{n_2}{n_1}, \quad \kappa = k_0 \sqrt{n_1^2 \sin^2\theta_i - n_2^2} \) intercepts the exponentially decaying field tail and excites a propagating wave across the low-index barrier. This frustrated total internal reflection (FTIR) tunnels optical energy across a classically forbidden gap at a rate decaying roughly as exp(−2κd) while preserving global flux conservation \( R = |r|^2, \quad T = \frac{n_2 \cos\theta_t}{n_1 \cos\theta_i} |t|^2 = 1 - R \) across the coupled double interface. Because the spatial Helmholtz equation inside the gap is mathematically isomorphic to the time-independent Schrödinger equation inside a rectangular potential barrier, FTIR realizes a direct optical analog of Quantum Tunneling and illuminates single-photon Wave-Particle Duality. Experimentally, evanescent coupling powers attenuated total reflection (ATR) infrared spectroscopy, total internal reflection fluorescence (TIRF) microscopy with sub-100-nanometer axial sectioning, prism couplers, and core-cladding confinement inside Optical Waveguides, Fibers and Photonic Crystals.

Extending single-boundary flux partitioning \( R = |r|^2, \quad T = \frac{n_2 \cos\theta_t}{n_1 \cos\theta_i} |t|^2 = 1 - R \) to stratified dielectric films turns Fresnel reflections into precision interference optics. Coating a substrate of index n2 with a transparent film of index nc and physical thickness d creates two normal-incidence reflected partial waves that cancel completely when their round-trip optical path equals half a vacuum wavelength λ0/2 and their reflection amplitudes match, fixing the quarter-wave anti-reflection condition \( n_c = \sqrt{n_1 n_2}, \quad d = \frac{\lambda_0}{4 n_c} \). For crown glass (n2 = 1.50) in air, the ideal index is nc ≈ 1.225; durable single-layer magnesium fluoride (MgF2, nc ≈ 1.38) reduces reflectance at 550 nanometers from 4.0 percent to 1.3 percent, while multi-layer dielectric stacks achieve sub-0.1-percent anti-reflection or 99.999-percent Bragg laser mirrors. Pairing quarter-wave interference stacks with oblique polarization splitting near \( \tan\theta_B = \frac{n_2}{n_1} \) further yields high-extinction thin-film polarizing beam splitters for precision interferometry and modern optical instrumentation.

fraunhofer-fresnel-diffraction.title: Fraunhofer and Fresnel Diffraction and Optical Resolution
fraunhofer-fresnel-diffraction.content:
Confining a coherent electromagnetic beam behind an opaque screen bearing a finite aperture bends wavefronts into the geometric shadow whenever the opening approaches the wavelength scale. For time-harmonic scalar fields obeying the Helmholtz reduction of the Electromagnetic Wave Equation, applying Green's theorem with Kirchhoff boundary conditions over an illuminated opening Σ expresses the downstream field at observation point P as a coherent sum of secondary spherical wavelets launched from every aperture point Q via \( U(P) = \frac{1}{i \lambda} \iint_{\Sigma} U(Q) \frac{e^{i k r}}{r} \cos\chi \, dS \). Here λ is the optical wavelength, k = 2π/λ is the wavenumber, r is the separation between Q and P, and the obliquity factor cos χ suppresses backward radiation while preserving the linear Principle of Superposition. Across an aperture of characteristic radius a viewed at axial distance z, the relative curvature of arriving wavefronts is controlled by the dimensionless Fresnel number \( F = \frac{a^2}{\lambda z} \), which counts how many half-wavelength zones of Wave Phase fit across the opening as seen from P.

When the observation plane lies close enough to the obstacle that \( F = \frac{a^2}{\lambda z} \) equals or exceeds unity, quadratic phase terms across the aperture cannot be neglected in \( U(P) = \frac{1}{i \lambda} \iint_{\Sigma} U(Q) \frac{e^{i k r}}{r} \cos\chi \, dS \), placing the wavefield in the near-field Fresnel regime. Expanding the path length r to second order in transverse aperture coordinates converts rectangular-edge integrals into cosine and sine Fresnel integrals whose parametric trajectory traces the Cornu spiral in the complex plane; chord lengths along this spiral directly predict the bright and dark fringes oscillating outside a straight edge's shadow and decaying monotonically inside it. Because curved wavefronts rephase continuously with propagation distance, near-field patterns evolve rapidly with z. Most famously, illuminating a perfectly circular opaque disk of radius a with Monochromatic Plane Waves yields constructive interference along the symmetry axis where every rim wavelet travels an identical path length, creating the Arago-Poisson bright spot at the dead center of the geometric shadow—a striking 1818 triumph for wave optics over corpuscular theory.

Moving into the far-field Fraunhofer regime where \( F = \frac{a^2}{\lambda z} \) falls far below unity—or equivalently placing a detector in the back focal plane of a thin converging lens—renders quadratic aperture phase variations negligible across Σ. Under this paraxial simplification, the spherical kernel collapses to a linear spatial phase factor determined by the transverse Propagation Vector components, reducing the diffracted field to the two-dimensional spatial transform \( U(x, y, z) = \frac{e^{i k z} e^{i \frac{k}{2z}(x^2 + y^2)}}{i \lambda z} \iint_{\Sigma} U(\xi, \eta, 0) e^{-i \frac{2\pi}{\lambda z}(x\xi + y\eta)} \, d\xi \, d\eta \). Apart from a spherical prefactor, far-field amplitudes therefore reproduce exact Fourier Transforms of the aperture transmission function U(ξ, η, 0). Integrating across a uniformly illuminated one-dimensional slit of width a yields the irradiance profile \( I(\theta) = I_0 \, \mathrm{sinc}^2\!\left(\frac{\pi a \sin\theta}{\lambda}\right) \), whose dark minima occur at a sin θ = mλ for nonzero integers m. Tightening spatial confinement a inevitably broadens angular spread Δθ ∼ λ/a, providing the classical wave counterpart to the quantum Uncertainty Principle.

Evaluating \( U(x, y, z) = \frac{e^{i k z} e^{i \frac{k}{2z}(x^2 + y^2)}}{i \lambda z} \iint_{\Sigma} U(\xi, \eta, 0) e^{-i \frac{2\pi}{\lambda z}(x\xi + y\eta)} \, d\xi \, d\eta \) over a circular aperture of diameter D = 2a introduces radial symmetry best solved through the Bessel family of Special Functions and Orthogonal Polynomials. Carrying out the azimuthal integral produces the circularly symmetric Airy pattern \( I(\theta) = I_0 \left[ \frac{2 J_1(k a \sin\theta)}{k a \sin\theta} \right]^2 \), where J1 is the first-order Bessel function of the first kind and 83.8 percent of total transmitted power concentrates inside the central Airy disk. Because the first zero of J1(u) lies at u ≈ 3.8317, Lord Rayleigh defined two incoherent point sources as just resolved when one central maximum falls onto the other's first dark ring, fixing the angular limit \( \theta_R = 1.22 \frac{\lambda}{D} \). In microscopy, Ernst Abbe showed that an objective of numerical aperture NA resolves lateral features down to λ/(2 NA); in astronomy, the 2.4-meter primary mirror of the Hubble Space Telescope reaches θR ≈ 0.05 arcseconds at 500 nanometers.

Extending single-slit geometry to a periodic diffraction grating of N identical rulings spaced by pitch d multiplies the broad single-slit envelope \( I(\theta) = I_0 \, \mathrm{sinc}^2\!\left(\frac{\pi a \sin\theta}{\lambda}\right) \) by a sharp N-slit interference factor whose principal maxima occur where adjacent grooves differ in optical path by an integer number of wavelengths m. For incidence angle θi and diffracted order angle θm, constructive reinforcement and the Rayleigh separation of adjacent wavelengths governed by \( \theta_R = 1.22 \frac{\lambda}{D} \) analogously yield the grating equation and chromatic resolving power \( d(\sin\theta_m + \sin\theta_i) = m\lambda, \quad R = \frac{\lambda}{\Delta\lambda} = m N \). Consequently, resolving spectral doublets separated by one part in 105 requires illuminating at least 105/m grooves coherently across the grating aperture. Meanwhile, Babinet's principle follows directly from linearity: summing fields transmitted by complementary opaque and open screens reproduces the unobstructed wave, guaranteeing identical off-axis far-field intensities for a thin wire and an equal-width slit.

Modern metrology and nanofabrication push these wave-optics boundaries across twelve orders of magnitude in wavelength. Semiconductor photolithography has migrated from deep-ultraviolet 193-nanometer immersion optics to extreme-ultraviolet (EUV) plasma sources at 13.5 nanometers, shrinking both λ in the Abbe resolution scale and the diffraction spot implied by \( \theta_R = 1.22 \frac{\lambda}{D} \) to pattern transistor gates below 10 nanometers. At angstrom wavelengths, hard X-rays scatter coherently off three-dimensional periodic atomic planes inside a Crystal Lattice, generalizing \( d(\sin\theta_m + \sin\theta_i) = m\lambda, \quad R = \frac{\lambda}{\Delta\lambda} = m N \) into Laue and Bragg crystallography that reconstructs molecular electron densities through inverse Fourier synthesis. Equally remarkably, Wave-Particle Duality ensures that electrons, thermal neutrons, and heavy fullerenes of de Broglie wavelength λ = h/p obey the exact same far-field transform \( U(x, y, z) = \frac{e^{i k z} e^{i \frac{k}{2z}(x^2 + y^2)}}{i \lambda z} \iint_{\Sigma} U(\xi, \eta, 0) e^{-i \frac{2\pi}{\lambda z}(x\xi + y\eta)} \, d\xi \, d\eta \), unifying classical optical resolution with quantum matter-wave interferometry.

optical-interferometry-coherence.title: Optical Interferometry, Fabry-Pérot Cavities and Coherence
optical-interferometry-coherence.content:
Superposing two electromagnetic wavefields displaced in space or delayed in time yields stationary irradiance fringes only when their electric-field fluctuations maintain stable statistical phase correlation across the detector integration window. By the Principle of Superposition, the net analytic signal at an observation screen sums the complex field amplitudes from both paths, while square-law photodetectors record the time-averaged optical irradiance proportional to the Poynting Vector. Expanding this squared modulus produces the sum of individual beam irradiances I1 + I2 plus an interference cross-term governed by the complex first-order mutual coherence function \( \Gamma_{12}(\tau) = \langle E^*(\mathbf{r}_1, t) E(\mathbf{r}_2, t + \tau) \rangle \) for stationary ergodic radiation. Normalizing by the geometric mean (Γ11(0)Γ22(0))1/2 defines the dimensionless complex degree of coherence γ12(τ), whose argument tracks the net Wave Phase shift and whose modulus directly fixes the Michelson fringe visibility \( V = \frac{I_{\max} - I_{\min}}{I_{\max} + I_{\min}} = |\gamma_{12}(\tau)| \) for equal-intensity beams, spanning from zero for mutually incoherent light to unity for ideal coherent interference.

Division-of-amplitude instruments such as the Michelson and Mach-Zehnder interferometers isolate longitudinal field correlations by splitting a collimated beam at a dielectric beamsplitter and recombining the two arms after a controllable optical path delay Δs = cτ. Under these self-coherence conditions (r1 = r2), the Wiener-Khinchin theorem establishes that the temporal autocorrelation γ(τ) and the normalized optical power spectral density S(ν) form an exact pair of Fourier Transforms. Any finite spectral bandwidth Δν therefore restricts the coherence time to τc ∼ 1/Δν, washing out interference fringe contrast in \( V = \frac{I_{\max} - I_{\min}}{I_{\max} + I_{\min}} = |\gamma_{12}(\tau)| \) once path delays exceed the temporal coherence length \( L_c = c \tau_c \approx \frac{\lambda^2}{\Delta\lambda} \). Broadband sunlight spanning roughly 300 nanometers around 550 nanometers sustains visible fringes over barely one micrometer—a short correlation gate exploited in optical coherence tomography—whereas low-pressure discharge lines reach several centimeters. Conversely, single-mode continuous-wave lasers governed by Laser Rate Equations and Population Inversion closely approach ideal Monochromatic Plane Waves with sub-kilohertz linewidths and coherence lengths exceeding hundreds of kilometers.

Even when relative path delays vanish (τ = 0), two apertures sampling an optical wavefield at transversely separated points r1 and r2 acquire spatial correlation that grows naturally with propagation distance from an incoherent thermal emitter. Because uncorrelated surface elements of a distant source radiate spherical wavelets that overlap coherently across the observation plane, the van Cittert-Zernike theorem proves that the equal-time spatial degree of coherence equals the normalized two-dimensional Fourier transform of the source angular intensity distribution I(θ), expressed as \( \gamma_{12}(0) = \frac{\iint I(\boldsymbol{\theta}) e^{-i k \boldsymbol{\theta} \cdot \Delta\mathbf{r}} \, d^2\theta}{\iint I(\boldsymbol{\theta}) \, d^2\theta} \) for baseline vector Δr = r2 − r1 and optical wavenumber k = 2π/λ. For a uniform circular stellar disk of angular diameter θs, fringe visibility first vanishes at baseline d = 1.22λ/θs, enabling Albert Michelson and Francis Pease in 1920 to measure Betelgeuse's 47-milliarcsecond angular diameter on Mount Wilson and anchoring modern long-baseline arrays such as CHARA and the VLTI. Whereas classical amplitude interferometry probes first-order correlations in \( \Gamma_{12}(\tau) = \langle E^*(\mathbf{r}_1, t) E(\mathbf{r}_2, t + \tau) \rangle \), measuring intensity-intensity correlations between separate photodetectors uncovers Hanbury Brown-Twiss photon bunching and nonclassical statistics analyzed in Quantum Optics and Photon Antibunching.

Superposing infinitely many partial waves undergoing successive reflections between two parallel, high-reflectivity dielectric mirrors transforms broad two-beam sinusoidal fringes into razor-sharp resonant transmission spikes. Inside a Fabry-Pérot etalon of mirror spacing L filled with a transparent medium of refractive index n, each consecutive round trip multiplies the complex field amplitude by the mirror intensity reflectivity R and adds an optical phase shift δ = (4πnL cosθ)/λ at internal angle θ. Summing this convergent geometric series of transmitted amplitudes for lossless identical mirrors yields the exact Airy transmission function \( T(\delta) = \frac{1}{1 + F \sin^2(\delta / 2)} \). Peak sharpness and inter-order rejection are controlled by the coefficient of finesse F and cavity finesse ℱ defined by \( \mathcal{F} \approx \frac{\pi \sqrt{R}}{1 - R}, \quad F = \frac{4R}{(1 - R)^2} \). As R approaches unity, destructive interference cancels off-resonant transmission nearly completely while integer resonances δ = 2πm transmit with unit efficiency despite individual mirrors reflecting more than 99.9 percent of incident optical power.

Adjacent longitudinal transmission maxima of \( T(\delta) = \frac{1}{1 + F \sin^2(\delta / 2)} \) repeat whenever the round-trip optical path equals an integer multiple of the wavelength, spacing consecutive resonant cavity modes uniformly in frequency by the free spectral range \( \Delta\nu_{\mathrm{FSR}} = \frac{c}{2 n L} \). Dividing this mode spacing by the finesse from \( \mathcal{F} \approx \frac{\pi \sqrt{R}}{1 - R}, \quad F = \frac{4R}{(1 - R)^2} \) fixes each resonance full width at half maximum at δν = ΔνFSR/ℱ, delivering a spectral resolving power ν/δν = mℱ that surpasses diffraction gratings by orders of magnitude for hyperfine atomic and Brillouin scattering spectroscopy. Modern ultrastable optical reference cavities machined from ultra-low-expansion glass or cryogenic single-crystal silicon employ ion-beam-sputtered Bragg coatings with reflectivity R > 0.99997, pushing cavity finesse above 105 and intracavity photon storage times into hundreds of microseconds. Pound-Drever-Hall phase locking to such narrow transmission fringes compresses continuous-wave laser linewidths below 10 millihertz, providing the phase-stable local oscillators required by strontium and ytterbium optical lattice clocks.

Interferometric phase sensitivity reaches its apex when closed-loop or resonant cavity topologies convert minute nonreciprocal or spacetime metric perturbations into measurable photocurrent signals. In a rotating ring Sagnac interferometer, counter-propagating beams enclosing area A acquire a relativistic transit-time phase difference proportional to angular velocity Ω, enabling drift-free fiber-optic gyroscopes for inertial navigation. At kilometer scales, the LIGO observatories embed 4-kilometer Fabry-Pérot cavities inside the orthogonal arms of a power-recycled Michelson interferometer to detect astrophysical Gravitational Waves. Operating with an arm finesse near 450 and free spectral range \( \Delta\nu_{\mathrm{FSR}} = \frac{c}{2 n L} \) of 37.5 kilohertz steepens the resonant phase slope of \( T(\delta) = \frac{1}{1 + F \sin^2(\delta / 2)} \) across hundreds of photon round trips, while a prestabilized 1064-nanometer Nd:YAG laser ensures \( L_c = c \tau_c \approx \frac{\lambda^2}{\Delta\lambda} \) far exceeds residual arm asymmetries. Injecting frequency-dependent Coherent and Squeezed Quantum States into the dark output port suppresses quantum shot noise, resolving differential mirror displacements below 10−19 meters.

geometric-optics-abcd-matrices.title: Geometric Optics, Fermat's Principle and ABCD Ray Matrices
geometric-optics-abcd-matrices.content:
When electromagnetic wavelengths shrink far below the scale of refractive inhomogeneities and aperture boundaries, the scalar Helmholtz reduction of the Electromagnetic Wave Equation admits the asymptotic trial solution U(r) = A(r)exp[ik0S(r)]. Substituting this ansatz and retaining the leading O(k02) terms as vacuum wavelength λ0 = 2π/k0 vanishes yields the eikonal equation \( | abla S(\mathbf{r})|^2 = n^2(\mathbf{r}) \), where the scalar eikonal S(r) defines surfaces of constant Wave Phase and local refractive index n(r) fixes the magnitude of the local Propagation Vector k = k0∇S. Because time-averaged electromagnetic energy flows normal to wavefronts in isotropic media, differentiating the unit ray tangent dr/ds = ∇S/n along arc length s produces the curved-medium ray equation \( rac{d}{ds}\!\left(n rac{d\mathbf{r}}{ds} ight) = abla n \). Spatial index gradients bend light continuously toward higher refractive index, explaining inferior desert mirages above sun-heated air layers and guiding optical pulses sinusoidally through graded-index (GRIN) glass cores in Optical Waveguides, Fibers and Photonic Crystals.

Identical ray trajectories follow directly from Pierre de Fermat's 1662 variational principle: among all smooth curves joining fixed endpoints A and B, a physical light ray renders the optical path length stationary according to \( \delta \int_{A}^{B} n(\mathbf{r})\,ds = 0 \). Applying the Calculus of Variations and Euler-Lagrange Equations to the optical Lagrangian L = n(r)|dr/dσ| immediately recovers the differential ray equation \( rac{d}{ds}\!\left(n rac{d\mathbf{r}}{ds} ight) = abla n \) together with Snell's law of refraction across discontinuous dielectric boundaries. This variational formulation establishes William Rowan Hamilton's celebrated optical-mechanical analogy: Fermat's stationary optical path mirrors Maupertuis's and Hamilton's Action Principle, with refractive index n(r) acting as mechanical momentum magnitude and \( | abla S(\mathbf{r})|^2 = n^2(\mathbf{r}) \) functioning as the time-independent Hamilton-Jacobi equation. Geometrically, rays trace Geodesics of the conformally curved optical metric dℓ2 = n2(r)ds2, while stationarity permits local maxima or saddle points alongside true minima at concave reflecting mirrors.

In rotationally symmetric optical instruments where rays stay close to the optical z-axis at small paraxial angles (&sin;θ ≈ θ), nonlinear trigonometric ray tracing linearizes into a 2 × 2 matrix algebra acting on transverse height and slope (y, θ)T. Free-space drifts of length d, spherical refracting interfaces of curvature radius R, and thin lenses of focal length f map input to output rays through \( egin{pmatrix} y_2 \ heta_2 \end{pmatrix} = egin{pmatrix} A & B \ C & D \end{pmatrix} egin{pmatrix} y_1 \ heta_1 \end{pmatrix}, \quad AD - BC = rac{n_1}{n_2} \), reducing arbitrarily complex multi-element optical cascades to ordered matrix multiplication. Unimodularity AD − BC = n1/n2 reflects canonical phase-space area preservation in Symplectic Geometry and Hamiltonian Manifolds, enforcing the Lagrange-Helmholtz optical invariant and conservation of optical étendue across every passive element. Cascading an object drift so, a thin lens, and an image drift si while requiring B = 0 for angle-independent point convergence yields the Gaussian thin-lens and lensmaker law \( rac{1}{s_o} + rac{1}{s_i} = rac{1}{f} = (n - 1)\left( rac{1}{R_1} - rac{1}{R_2} ight) \), establishing both lateral magnification and focal power directly from glass index and surface curvatures.

Cascading identical matrix blocks repeatedly models periodic lens waveguides and two-mirror Fabry-Pérot cavities central to Laser Rate Equations and Population Inversion. For a closed round trip of optical length 2L beginning and ending in the same medium (n1 = n2), the round-trip transfer matrix M in \( egin{pmatrix} y_2 \ heta_2 \end{pmatrix} = egin{pmatrix} A & B \ C & D \end{pmatrix} egin{pmatrix} y_1 \ heta_1 \end{pmatrix}, \quad AD - BC = rac{n_1}{n_2} \) is strictly unimodular (det M = 1), so its characteristic polynomial depends solely on the matrix trace A + D. By Sylvester's theorem from linear Eigenvalue Problems, ray heights stay bounded over arbitrary round trips if and only if both eigenvalues lie on the unit circle, requiring |A + D| ≤ 2. Evaluating this trace for spherical mirrors of curvature radii R1 and R2 separated by cavity length L yields the resonator stability criterion \( 0 \le g_1 g_2 \le 1, \quad g_i = 1 - rac{L}{R_i} \). Symmetric confocal (g1 = g2 = 0), concentric, hemispherical, and planar cavities occupy the stability boundaries, whereas unstable resonators intentionally expand beams to fill large gain volumes in high-power industrial lasers.

The identical 2 × 2 paraxial matrix elements govern finite-wavelength diffracting laser beams once ray height and slope are unified into the complex beam parameter q(z) = z + izR. Solving the paraxial Helmholtz equation for the fundamental TEM00 Gaussian mode links Rayleigh range zR = πnw02/λ, minimum beam waist w0, wavefront curvature radius R(z), and transverse spot radius w(z) through Herwig Kogelnik's bilinear ABCD law \( q_2 = rac{A q_1 + B}{C q_1 + D}, \quad rac{1}{q(z)} = rac{1}{R(z)} - rac{i \lambda}{\pi n w^2(z)} \). Enforcing round-trip self-consistency (q2 = q1) inside a laser resonator produces a physical Gaussian eigenmode with finite real spot size w if and only if \( 0 \le g_1 g_2 \le 1, \quad g_i = 1 - rac{L}{R_i} \) holds strictly, fixing waist location and divergence automatically. As optical wavelength λ approaches zero, the imaginary diffraction term vanishes and q(z) collapses cleanly onto the spherical wavefront curvature R(z), reconnecting paraxial wave optics directly to the constant-phase surfaces of \( | abla S(\mathbf{r})|^2 = n^2(\mathbf{r}) \).

At high numerical apertures or wide off-axis field angles, expanding &sin;θ = θ − θ3/6 + … inside the optical path length of \( \delta \int_{A}^{B} n(\mathbf{r})\,ds = 0 \) produces fourth-order wavefront departures beyond the ideal paraxial focus of \( rac{1}{s_o} + rac{1}{s_i} = rac{1}{f} = (n - 1)\left( rac{1}{R_1} - rac{1}{R_2} ight) \). Philipp Ludwig von Seidel classified these third-order transverse ray errors in axisymmetric systems into five primary monochromatic aberrations: spherical aberration, focusing marginal rays closer than paraxial rays; coma, flaring off-axis point images asymmetrically; astigmatism, separating sagittal and tangential focal lines; Petzval field curvature, curving the sharp focal surface into a paraboloid; and pincushion or barrel distortion, shifting lateral magnification radially across the image plane. Optical designers balance these five Seidel sums across compound microscope objectives, cemented achromatic doublets, and precision aspheric mirrors achieving diffraction-limited resolution across microscopy, lithography, and astronomy while preserving the symplectic phase-space invariant of \( egin{pmatrix} y_2 \ heta_2 \end{pmatrix} = egin{pmatrix} A & B \ C & D \end{pmatrix} egin{pmatrix} y_1 \ heta_1 \end{pmatrix}, \quad AD - BC = rac{n_1}{n_2} \).

fourier-optics-spatial-filtering.title: Fourier Optics, Transfer Functions and Spatial Filtering
fourier-optics-spatial-filtering.hero_equation: H(f_x, f_y; z) = \exp\!\left[ i k z \sqrt{1 - (\lambda f_x)^2 - (\lambda f_y)^2} \right]
fourier-optics-spatial-filtering.content:
Monochromatic scalar diffraction of a transverse optical field U(x, y, z) governed by the Helmholtz reduction of the Electromagnetic Wave Equation forms a linear shift-invariant system of Linear Operators obeying the Principle of Superposition. Decomposing the complex field across the input plane z = 0 via two-dimensional Fourier Transforms resolves any wavefront into Monochromatic Plane Waves indexed by spatial frequencies (fx, fy) and direction cosines (λfx, λfy) along the Propagation Vector k of magnitude k = 2π/λ. Advancing each angular component across homogeneous free space of distance z multiplies its spectrum by the exact free-space transfer function \( H(f_x, f_y; z) = \exp\!\left[ i k z \sqrt{1 - (\lambda f_x)^2 - (\lambda f_y)^2} \right] \). Modes inside the circle fx2 + fy2 ≤ 1/λ2 acquire pure phase shifts and propagate undamped to the far field, whereas higher spatial frequencies become exponentially damped evanescent waves decaying within a wavelength, enforcing the sub-wavelength diffraction barrier. Expanding the square root for paraxial angles yields the Fresnel transfer function \( H_{\mathrm{F}}(f_x, f_y; z) = e^{i k z} \exp\!\left[ -i \pi \lambda z \left( f_x^2 + f_y^2 \right) \right] \).

A thin spherical refractive lens of focal length f retards paraxial rays according to radially varying glass thickness, imprinting a quadratic Wave Phase delay captured by the amplitude transmittance \( t_l(x, y) = \exp\!\left[ -i \frac{k}{2 f} \left( x^2 + y^2 \right) \right] \). When a coherently illuminated transparency U0(x0, y0) sits in the front focal plane, cascading Fresnel propagation \( H_{\mathrm{F}}(f_x, f_y; z) = e^{i k z} \exp\!\left[ -i \pi \lambda z \left( f_x^2 + f_y^2 \right) \right] \) over distance f, lens transmission, and a second focal propagation cancels every outer quadratic phase factor identically. The back focal plane therefore realizes an exact physical two-dimensional Fourier transform \( U_f(x_f, y_f) = \frac{1}{i \lambda f} \iint_{-\infty}^{\infty} U_0(x_0, y_0) \exp\!\left[ -i \frac{2\pi}{\lambda f} (x_f x_0 + y_f y_0) \right] dx_0 \, dy_0 \), mapping spatial frequencies onto transverse coordinates xf = λffx, yf = λffy. Ernst Abbe established in 1873 that microscope imaging is a two-stage diffraction and Fourier Synthesis process: the objective fans object periodicities into discrete angular orders across its back focal plane, and a second lens recombines those spatial harmonics into an inverted real image, so any aperture blocking high diffraction orders permanently erases fine structural detail.

Cascading a second identical lens one focal length behind the back focal plane builds a telecentric 4f optical correlator whose central Fourier plane exposes \( U_f(x_f, y_f) = \frac{1}{i \lambda f} \iint_{-\infty}^{\infty} U_0(x_0, y_0) \exp\!\left[ -i \frac{2\pi}{\lambda f} (x_f x_0 + y_f y_0) \right] dx_0 \, dy_0 \) to physical amplitude or phase masks. Multiplying the focal-plane spectrum by a pupil filter M(xf, yf) executes a real-space two-dimensional convolution at the speed of light, mirroring impulse-response propagation from Green's Functions. A centered pinhole acts as a low-pass spatial filter stripping laser speckle and halftone pixel grids, whereas an opaque central stop blocking the undiffracted zero-frequency (DC) order performs high-pass dark-field filtering that accentuates sharp edges and boundaries. Because diffraction and lensing strictly preserve linearity via \( H(f_x, f_y; z) = \exp\!\left[ i k z \sqrt{1 - (\lambda f_x)^2 - (\lambda f_y)^2} \right] \) and \( t_l(x, y) = \exp\!\left[ -i \frac{k}{2 f} \left( x^2 + y^2 \right) \right] \), complex VanderLugt matched filters in the 4f Fourier plane perform parallel optical cross-correlation for real-time pattern recognition.

Unstained living cells, bacteria, and thin biological membranes behave as transparent phase objects whose transmittance t(x, y) = exp[iφ(x, y)] ≈ 1 + iφ(x, y) for weak phase shifts |φ| ≪ 1 modulates optical phase while leaving intensity |t|2 ≈ 1 uniform and invisible under conventional bright-field microscopy. In 1934, Frits Zernike—awarded the 1953 Nobel Prize in Physics—recognized from \( U_f(x_f, y_f) = \frac{1}{i \lambda f} \iint_{-\infty}^{\infty} U_0(x_0, y_0) \exp\!\left[ -i \frac{2\pi}{\lambda f} (x_f x_0 + y_f y_0) \right] dx_0 \, dy_0 \) that the strong undiffracted background focuses onto the central DC spot while the weak scattered phase wave iφ(x, y) spreads into higher spatial frequencies in π/2 phase quadrature. Placing a microscopic quarter-wave dielectric plate at the 4f origin shifts only the DC order by ±π/2, bringing background and scattered light into direct collinear interference and converting invisible refractive-index variations linearly into measurable irradiance \( I_{\mathrm{Z}}(x, y) \approx I_0 \left[ 1 + 2 \phi(x, y) \right] \). Combining phase-plate attenuation with \( t_l(x, y) = \exp\!\left[ -i \frac{k}{2 f} \left( x^2 + y^2 \right) \right] \) renders living intracellular organelles clearly visible without toxic chemical staining.

Practical imaging performance depends decisively on illumination coherence. Under spatially coherent light, an aberration-free lens is linear in complex field amplitude, and its coherent transfer function (CTF) equals the scaled pupil aperture P(λdifx, λdify) with an abrupt step cutoff at fcoh = NA/λ for numerical aperture NA and image distance di. Under spatially incoherent illumination, uncorrelated source emitters add strictly in irradiance; the system is linear in intensity, and its normalized optical transfer function (OTF) equals the two-dimensional autocorrelation of the generalized pupil function \( \mathcal{H}(f_x, f_y) = \frac{\iint P(\xi, \eta) P^*(\xi - \lambda d_i f_x, \eta - \lambda d_i f_y) \, d\xi \, d\eta}{\iint |P(\xi, \eta)|^2 \, d\xi \, d\eta} \). Its modulus defines the modulation transfer function MTF = |OTF|, falling monotonically from unity to an incoherent cutoff fc = 2NA/λ—twice the coherent cutoff, without coherent edge ringing. Wavefront aberrations enter the pupil phase inside \( \mathcal{H}(f_x, f_y) = \frac{\iint P(\xi, \eta) P^*(\xi - \lambda d_i f_x, \eta - \lambda d_i f_y) \, d\xi \, d\eta}{\iint |P(\xi, \eta)|^2 \, d\xi \, d\eta} \) and strictly depress MTF below the diffraction limit, while axial defocus adds quadratic phase curvature akin to \( H_{\mathrm{F}}(f_x, f_y; z) = e^{i k z} \exp\!\left[ -i \pi \lambda z \left( f_x^2 + f_y^2 \right) \right] \) that can reverse contrast like sign inversion in \( I_{\mathrm{Z}}(x, y) \approx I_0 \left[ 1 + 2 \phi(x, y) \right] \).

Because square-law photodetectors and photographic emulsions record only time-averaged irradiance, capturing an object wavefront O(x, y) directly discards its phase and three-dimensional parallax. Dennis Gabor (1948) solved this loss by interfering the scattered object wave with a coherent reference wave R; Emmett Leith and Juris Upatnieks (1962) perfected laser holography by tilting the reference beam onto an off-axis spatial carrier frequency, yielding the recorded hologram intensity \( I_h(x, y) = |R|^2 + |O(x, y)|^2 + R^* O(x, y) + R O^*(x, y) \). Re-illuminating the transparency with R diffracts the cross-terms R*O and RO* into an exact three-dimensional virtual image and a phase-conjugate real image separated cleanly in spatial-frequency space from the on-axis DC terms |R|2 + |O|2, with volumetric wavefront reconstruction governed by \( H(f_x, f_y; z) = \exp\!\left[ i k z \sqrt{1 - (\lambda f_x)^2 - (\lambda f_y)^2} \right] \). Digital holography, adaptive optics, and quantitative phase microscopy invert \( I_h(x, y) = |R|^2 + |O(x, y)|^2 + R^* O(x, y) + R O^*(x, y) \) and \( \mathcal{H}(f_x, f_y) = \frac{\iint P(\xi, \eta) P^*(\xi - \lambda d_i f_x, \eta - \lambda d_i f_y) \, d\xi \, d\eta}{\iint |P(\xi, \eta)|^2 \, d\xi \, d\eta} \) computationally, while encoding three-dimensional optical fields onto a two-dimensional interference boundary inspired the Holographic Principle in gravitational physics.

formulas.title: Snell's Law of Optical Refraction
formulas.description: Relates the angle of incidence $\theta_i$ in a medium of refractive index $n_1$ to the angle of refraction $\theta_t$ in an adjacent medium of refractive index $n_2$ by enforcing tangential wavevector continuity across a planar interface.
formulas.conceptual_definition: Snell's law $n_1 \sin\theta_i = n_2 \sin\theta_t$ expresses tangential phase matching of electromagnetic plane waves across a flat boundary between two isotropic transparent dielectrics.
formulas.intuitive_summary: Because wave crests must stay joined along the boundary without slipping, light bends toward the normal when slowing down in a denser medium and away from the normal when speeding up.
formulas.interpretation: Since the wavevector magnitude in a medium of index $n$ is $k = n k_0 = n\omega/c$, equality of the tangential component $k_\parallel = k_1 \sin\theta_i = k_2 \sin\theta_t$ cancels $k_0$ and produces $n_1 \sin\theta_i = n_2 \sin\theta_t$. Equivalently, Fermat's principle of stationary optical path length yields the same refraction law.
formulas.symmetry_origin: Follows directly from continuous spatial translation invariance parallel to the planar interface, which conserves the tangential component of photon momentum $\hbar k_\parallel$ across the boundary.
formulas.limits_and_boundary: At normal incidence ($\theta_i = 0$), $\theta_t = 0$ and the ray passes undeflected. When $n_1 > n_2$ and $\sin\theta_i > n_2/n_1$, no real angle $\theta_t$ exists and total internal reflection occurs.

formulas.title: Fresnel s-Polarized (TE) Amplitude Reflection Coefficient
formulas.description: Gives the complex ratio $r_s = E_{r,s}/E_{i,s}$ of reflected to incident electric-field amplitudes for a transverse-electric (s-polarized) plane wave whose electric field oscillates perpendicular to the plane of incidence at a nonmagnetic dielectric interface.
formulas.conceptual_definition: The s-polarized Fresnel reflection coefficient quantifies the exact amplitude and phase of the reflected electric field when the optical electric vector lies parallel to the interface and perpendicular to the plane of incidence.
formulas.intuitive_summary: When light's electric field oscillates parallel to a glass surface, reflection grows steadily stronger from normal incidence to grazing angles and never vanishes at any intermediate angle.
formulas.interpretation: Derived from continuity of $E_\parallel$ ($E_i + E_r = E_t$) and $H_\parallel$ ($n_1(E_i - E_r)\cos\theta_i = n_2 E_t \cos\theta_t$) for nonmagnetic media ($\mu_1 = \mu_2 = \mu_0$). When $n_2 > n_1$, the numerator is strictly negative for all real $\theta_i$, producing a $\pi$-radian phase inversion upon external reflection.
formulas.symmetry_origin: Follows from the tangential boundary conditions of Maxwell's equations for a planar nonmagnetic interface combined with mirror symmetry perpendicular to the plane of incidence.
formulas.limits_and_boundary: At normal incidence ($\theta_i = \theta_t = 0$), $r_s = (n_1 - n_2)/(n_1 + n_2)$. At grazing incidence ($\theta_i \to \pi/2$), $\cos\theta_i \to 0$ so $r_s \to -1$ and reflectance approaches 100 percent. Above the critical angle ($n_1 > n_2$), $\cos\theta_t$ is purely imaginary and $|r_s| = 1$.

formulas.title: Fresnel p-Polarized (TM) Amplitude Reflection Coefficient
formulas.description: Gives the complex ratio $r_p = E_{r,p}/E_{i,p}$ of reflected to incident electric-field amplitudes for a transverse-magnetic (p-polarized) plane wave whose electric field lies inside the plane of incidence at a nonmagnetic dielectric interface.
formulas.conceptual_definition: The p-polarized Fresnel reflection coefficient determines the reflected amplitude and phase for light polarized parallel to the plane of incidence, exhibiting an exact zero at Brewster's angle.
formulas.intuitive_summary: When light's electric field oscillates inside the plane of incidence, reflection drops all the way to zero at Brewster's angle before climbing back to total reflection at grazing incidence.
formulas.interpretation: Matching tangential magnetic fields ($n_1(E_i + E_r) = n_2 E_t$) and tangential electric fields ($(E_i - E_r)\cos\theta_i = E_t \cos\theta_t$) yields $r_p = (n_2 \cos\theta_i - n_1 \cos\theta_t)/(n_2 \cos\theta_i + n_1 \cos\theta_t)$. Crossing Brewster's angle reverses the sign of the numerator, introducing a $\pi$ phase jump.
formulas.symmetry_origin: Arises from tangential continuity of Maxwell's fields at a flat nonmagnetic dielectric boundary under transverse-magnetic polarization decomposition.
formulas.limits_and_boundary: At normal incidence ($\theta_i = \theta_t = 0$), $r_p = (n_2 - n_1)/(n_2 + n_1)$ matches $|r_s|$. At Brewster's angle ($\tan\theta_B = n_2/n_1$), $r_p = 0$. At grazing incidence ($\theta_i \to \pi/2$), $r_p \to -1$, and above the critical angle ($n_1 > n_2$), $|r_p| = 1$.

formulas.title: Fresnel Reflectance, Transmittance and Energy Flux Conservation
formulas.description: Expresses the power reflectance $R$ and transmittance $T$ across a lossless planar dielectric interface in terms of the Fresnel amplitude reflection and transmission coefficients $r$ and $t$, enforcing conservation of the normal Poynting flux ($R + T = 1$).
formulas.conceptual_definition: Interface reflectance and transmittance measure the fractions of incident electromagnetic power per unit boundary area reflected back into medium 1 and transmitted into medium 2.
formulas.intuitive_summary: Every watt of optical power arriving at a transparent surface is cleanly split between the reflected beam and the refracted beam, accounting for how refraction changes both beam speed and beam width.
formulas.interpretation: Because the time-averaged Poynting flux magnitude in a nonmagnetic dielectric is $S = \frac{1}{2}\varepsilon_0 c n |E|^2$ and a beam of width $A \cos\theta_i$ refracts to width $A \cos\theta_t$, the transmitted-to-incident power ratio picks up the factor $(n_2 \cos\theta_t)/(n_1 \cos\theta_i)$. Substituting either $(r_s, t_s)$ or $(r_p, t_p)$ verifies $R + T = 1$ identically.
formulas.symmetry_origin: Derived directly from Poynting's theorem and time-translation invariance of the source-free electromagnetic energy density in lossless linear media.
formulas.limits_and_boundary: At normal incidence, $T = (n_2/n_1)|t|^2 = 4 n_1 n_2 / (n_1 + n_2)^2$. Above the critical angle in total internal reflection, $\cos\theta_t$ is purely imaginary so $R = 1$ and the time-averaged normal transmittance $T$ vanishes.

formulas.title: Brewster's Polarizing Angle
formulas.description: Defines the unique incidence angle $\theta_B$ at a planar nonmagnetic dielectric interface where the p-polarized (TM) Fresnel reflection amplitude $r_p$ vanishes identically, rendering reflected light purely s-polarized.
formulas.conceptual_definition: Brewster's angle $\theta_B = \arctan(n_2/n_1)$ is the incidence angle at which the reflected and refracted rays are mutually perpendicular and p-polarized reflection disappears completely.
formulas.intuitive_summary: At Brewster's angle, the electrons oscillating inside the glass point straight along the reflected beam direction; because an oscillating dipole cannot radiate along its own axis, no p-polarized light reflects.
formulas.interpretation: Setting the numerator $n_2 \cos\theta_i - n_1 \cos\theta_t = 0$ together with Snell's law $n_1 \sin\theta_i = n_2 \sin\theta_t$ gives $\sin\theta_i \cos\theta_i = \sin\theta_t \cos\theta_t$, whose nontrivial solution is $\theta_i + \theta_t = \pi/2$. Thus $\sin\theta_t = \cos\theta_B$ and $\tan\theta_B = n_2/n_1$ (yielding $56.3^\circ$ for air-to-crown-glass with $n_2 = 1.50$).
formulas.symmetry_origin: Originates from the transverse vector nature of electromagnetic dipole radiation, whose angular intensity pattern $\sin^2\psi$ has an exact symmetry null along the dipole oscillation axis ($\psi = 0$).
formulas.limits_and_boundary: Exists for both external ($n_1 < n_2$, $\theta_B > 45^\circ$) and internal ($n_1 > n_2$, $\theta_B < 45^\circ$) nonmagnetic incidence, always satisfying $\theta_{B,\mathrm{int}} < \theta_c$. In absorbing media with complex $n_2$, $R_p$ reaches a nonzero minimum at the pseudo-Brewster angle.

formulas.title: Total Internal Reflection Critical Angle and Evanescent Decay Constant
formulas.description: Specifies the critical angle $\theta_c$ for total internal reflection from a denser medium ($n_1 > n_2$) and the exponential attenuation constant $\kappa$ governing the surface-bound evanescent wave decaying as $e^{-\kappa z}$ into the rarer medium for $\theta_i > \theta_c$.
formulas.conceptual_definition: Above the critical angle $\sin\theta_c = n_2/n_1$, no propagating refracted wave can satisfy tangential phase matching, so all optical power reflects while an exponentially localized evanescent field penetrates medium 2 over depth $1/\kappa$.
formulas.intuitive_summary: Past the critical angle, light cannot escape into the lower-index medium and reflects completely, yet a faint electromagnetic field still leaks a fraction of a wavelength across the boundary before dying away exponentially.
formulas.interpretation: In medium 2, the normal wavevector component satisfies $k_{2z}^2 = n_2^2 k_0^2 - k_\parallel^2 = k_0^2(n_2^2 - n_1^2 \sin^2\theta_i)$. For $\theta_i > \theta_c = \arcsin(n_2/n_1)$, $k_{2z} = i\kappa$ is purely imaginary, converting $e^{i k_{2z} z}$ into $e^{-\kappa z}$. For crown glass ($n_1 = 1.50$) into air ($n_2 = 1.00$), $\theta_c \approx 41.8^\circ$.
formulas.symmetry_origin: Follows from the dispersion relation $k_\parallel^2 + k_{2z}^2 = n_2^2 k_0^2$ combined with tangential momentum conservation across the planar interface.
formulas.limits_and_boundary: As $\theta_i \to \theta_c^+$, $\kappa \to 0$ and the evanescent penetration depth $1/\kappa$ diverges as the wave grazes the surface. At grazing incidence ($\theta_i \to \pi/2$), $\kappa$ reaches its maximum $k_0 \sqrt{n_1^2 - n_2^2}$.

formulas.title: Quarter-Wave Anti-Reflection Coating Condition
formulas.description: Specifies the optimal refractive index $n_c$ and physical thickness $d$ of a single-layer dielectric thin film on a substrate of index $n_2$ in ambient medium $n_1$ to eliminate normal-incidence reflection at design wavelength $\lambda_0$ by destructive interference.
formulas.conceptual_definition: A quarter-wave anti-reflection coating cancels specular reflection completely when its optical thickness $n_c d$ equals $\lambda_0/4$ and its index $n_c$ equals the geometric mean $\sqrt{n_1 n_2}$ of the bounding media.
formulas.intuitive_summary: A thin transparent film one quarter of a wavelength thick makes light reflected from the top and bottom surfaces arrive exactly half a cycle out of step, and choosing the geometric-mean index makes their strengths equal so they cancel completely.
formulas.interpretation: When $n_1 < n_c < n_2$, both interface reflections undergo a $\pi$ phase flip, so the round-trip optical path $2 n_c d = \lambda_0/2$ supplies the exact $\pi$ relative phase shift needed for destructive interference. Equalizing the two Fresnel amplitudes $(n_1 - n_c)/(n_1 + n_c) = (n_c - n_2)/(n_c + n_2)$ uniquely solves to $n_c = \sqrt{n_1 n_2}$.
formulas.symmetry_origin: Follows from coherent wave superposition and the transfer-matrix impedance matching condition across a stratified planar dielectric stack.
formulas.limits_and_boundary: At exact design wavelength $\lambda_0$ and normal incidence with $n_c = \sqrt{n_1 n_2}$, reflectance drops to $R = 0$ ($T = 1$). Away from $\lambda_0$ or when using practical coatings such as $\mathrm{MgF}_2$ ($n_c \approx 1.38$ on glass $n_2 = 1.50$), residual reflectance remains $R = [(n_c^2 - n_1 n_2)/(n_c^2 + n_1 n_2)]^2 \approx 1.3\%$.

formulas.title: Huygens-Fresnel Scalar Diffraction Integral
formulas.description: Expresses the complex scalar optical field $U(P)$ at an observation point $P$ as the coherent integral over an illuminated aperture $\Sigma$ of secondary spherical wavelets $e^{ikr}/r$ weighted by the aperture field $U(Q)$ and obliquity factor $\cos\chi$.
formulas.conceptual_definition: The Huygens-Fresnel diffraction integral quantifies scalar wave propagation past an aperture by superposing spherical Green's-function wavelets emitted from every point of the open wavefront.
formulas.intuitive_summary: Every point inside an open aperture acts like a tiny point lamp emitting expanding spherical ripples; the brightness anywhere downstream comes from adding all those overlapping ripples with their exact phases.
formulas.interpretation: Derived from the time-harmonic Helmholtz equation $(\nabla^2 + k^2)U = 0$ via Green's second identity and the Kirchhoff or Rayleigh-Sommerfeld boundary conditions, the factor $1/(i\lambda)$ introduces the $\pi/2$ Gouy-type phase shift needed for plane waves to propagate undistorted in free space, while $\cos\chi$ weights forward propagation over oblique emission.
formulas.symmetry_origin: Follows from the linearity and rotational isotropy of the three-dimensional Helmholtz operator $(\nabla^2 + k^2)$ whose free-space Green's function is the spherical wave $e^{ikr}/(4\pi r)$.
formulas.limits_and_boundary: Valid when the aperture dimensions and observation distance greatly exceed the optical wavelength ($r \gg \lambda$) and polarization coupling at the screen edges is negligible; reduces to geometric optics as $\lambda \to 0$.

U(P).name: Diffracted Scalar Optical Field
U(P).description: Complex monochromatic scalar field amplitude evaluated at the downstream observation point $P$.

U(Q).name: Aperture Scalar Optical Field
U(Q).description: Complex monochromatic scalar field amplitude at source point $Q$ lying inside the aperture surface $\Sigma$.

\\lambda.name: Optical Wavelength

\\chi.name: Obliquity Angle

dS.name: Aperture Area Element
dS.description: Infinitesimal surface area element integrated across the open aperture $\Sigma$.

formulas.title: Fresnel Number
formulas.description: Defines the dimensionless Fresnel number $F = a^2 / (\lambda z)$ for an aperture of characteristic radius or half-width $a$, optical wavelength $\lambda$, and axial propagation distance $z$, separating near-field Fresnel diffraction from far-field Fraunhofer diffraction.
formulas.conceptual_definition: The Fresnel number measures the maximum quadratic phase curvature across an aperture in half-wavelength units, serving as the universal dimensionless parameter classifying diffraction regimes.
formulas.intuitive_summary: Compare the aperture area $a^2$ against the product of wavelength and distance $\lambda z$: when $F$ is large you are in the near field where shadows stay sharp and curved fringes shift rapidly; when $F$ is tiny you are in the far field.
formulas.interpretation: In the paraxial expansion $r \approx z + [(x-\xi)^2 + (y-\eta)^2]/(2z)$, the quadratic aperture phase $k(\xi^2 + \eta^2)/(2z)$ reaches $\pi a^2 / (\lambda z) = \pi F$ at the rim. Thus $F$ directly counts the number of half-period Fresnel zones visible through the aperture from an on-axis point at distance $z$.
formulas.symmetry_origin: Arises from dimensionless scaling invariance of the paraxial Helmholtz propagation equation under transverse length rescaling $\xi \to s\xi$ and axial rescaling $z \to s^2 z$.
formulas.limits_and_boundary: When $F \ll 1$, quadratic phase curvature is negligible and far-field Fraunhofer diffraction holds; when $F \gtrsim 1$, near-field Fresnel diffraction applies; as $F \to \infty$ ($\lambda \to 0$), wave diffraction collapses into geometric ray shadows.

F.name: Fresnel Number
F.description: Dimensionless ratio distinguishing near-field Fresnel diffraction ($F \gtrsim 1$) from far-field Fraunhofer diffraction ($F \ll 1$).

a.name: Characteristic Aperture Radius
a.description: Radius or half-width characterizing the transverse spatial extent of the diffracting aperture.

\\lambda.name: Optical Wavelength
\\lambda.description: Wavelength of the illuminating monochromatic radiation.

z.name: Propagation Distance
z.description: Axial distance between the aperture plane and the observation screen.

formulas.title: Fraunhofer Far-Field Fourier Diffraction Integral
formulas.equation: U(x, y, z) = \frac{e^{i k z} e^{i \frac{k}{2z}(x^2 + y^2)}}{i \lambda z} \iint_{\Sigma} U(\xi, \eta, 0) e^{-i \frac{2\pi}{\lambda z}(x\xi + y\eta)} \, d\xi \, d\eta
formulas.description: Expresses the far-field Fraunhofer scalar wave amplitude $U(x, y, z)$ as a spherical phase prefactor multiplying the exact two-dimensional spatial Fourier transform of the aperture field $U(\xi, \eta, 0)$ evaluated at spatial frequencies $f_x = x/(\lambda z)$ and $f_y = y/(\lambda z)$.
formulas.conceptual_definition: In the far-field limit $F \ll 1$, optical diffraction acts as an analog physical computer that performs an exact two-dimensional Fourier transform of the aperture transmission function.
formulas.intuitive_summary: Far away from an aperture—or right at the focal plane of a lens—the diffraction pattern is simply the spatial frequency spectrum of the aperture's shape.
formulas.interpretation: Dropping the quadratic aperture phase factor $e^{i k(\xi^2 + \eta^2)/(2z)}$ when $k(\xi^2 + \eta^2)/(2z) \ll 1$ leaves only the linear Fourier kernel $e^{-i 2\pi (x\xi + y\eta)/(\lambda z)}$. Because the prefactor outside the integral has unit modulus up to $1/(\lambda z)$, the observable irradiance $I(x,y,z) \propto |U|^2$ depends purely on the squared modulus of the aperture's spatial Fourier transform.
formulas.symmetry_origin: Reflects transverse translational invariance of free-space propagation in the paraxial limit, which diagonalizes the propagation operator in the plane-wave Fourier basis.
formulas.limits_and_boundary: Valid in the far-field regime $z \gg a^2/\lambda$ ($F \ll 1$) and paraxial angles $x, y \ll z$, or exactly in the back focal plane of an ideal aberration-free thin lens of focal length $f$ with $z$ replaced by $f$.

U(x, y, z).name: Far-Field Diffracted Amplitude
U(x, y, z).description: Complex optical field amplitude at transverse observation coordinates $(x, y)$ and axial distance $z$.

U(\\xi, \\eta, 0).name: Aperture Field Distribution
U(\\xi, \\eta, 0).description: Complex optical field immediately behind the aperture plane at transverse source coordinates $(\xi, \eta)$.

\\lambda.name: Optical Wavelength
