z.name: Observation Distance
z.description: Axial distance from the aperture plane to the far-field observation plane.

x.name: Horizontal Observation Coordinate
x.description: Transverse horizontal position in the far-field observation plane.

y.name: Vertical Observation Coordinate
y.description: Transverse vertical position in the far-field observation plane.

\\xi.name: Horizontal Aperture Coordinate
\\xi.description: Transverse horizontal integration coordinate across the aperture.

\\eta.name: Vertical Aperture Coordinate
\\eta.description: Transverse vertical integration coordinate across the aperture.

formulas.title: Single-Slit Fraunhofer Diffraction Intensity
formulas.description: Gives the far-field angular irradiance distribution $I(\theta)$ produced by monochromatic light of wavelength $\lambda$ diffracting through a uniformly illuminated single slit of width $a$, expressed using the unnormalized sinc function $\mathrm{sinc}(\beta) = (\sin\beta)/\beta$.
formulas.conceptual_definition: The single-slit diffraction pattern is the squared Fourier transform of a rectangular top-hat aperture, concentrating most energy in a central maximum of angular width $2\lambda/a$ flanked by rapidly decaying secondary fringes.
formulas.intuitive_summary: Squeezing light through a narrow slit fans it out into a bright central band bordered by alternating dark nulls and fainter side lobes; the narrower the slit, the wider the central band spreads.
formulas.interpretation: Setting $\beta = \pi a \sin\theta / \lambda$, the zeros of $\sin\beta$ occur whenever $a \sin\theta = m\lambda$ ($m = \pm 1, \pm 2, \dots$), corresponding to dividing the slit into $2|m|$ equal strips that cancel pairwise by destructive interference. The first side maxima reach only 4.7 percent of the central peak irradiance $I_0$.
formulas.symmetry_origin: Follows from the Fourier duality between a symmetric one-dimensional rectangular boxcar function of width $a$ and the even function $\mathrm{sinc}(\beta)$.
formulas.limits_and_boundary: As $\theta \to 0$, $\mathrm{sinc}(\beta) \to 1$ so $I(0) = I_0$; when $a \gg \lambda$, the central lobe narrows into a sharp geometric beam; when $a < \lambda$, no off-axis dark minima exist for real angles $|\sin\theta| \le 1$.

I(\\theta).name: Diffracted Optical Irradiance
I(\\theta).description: Time-averaged optical power per unit area measured at diffraction angle $\theta$.

I_0.name: On-Axis Peak Irradiance
I_0.description: Maximum optical irradiance at the central forward direction $\theta = 0$.

a.name: Slit Width
a.description: Transverse width of the illuminated rectangular slit aperture.

\\theta.name: Diffraction Angle
\\theta.description: Angle measured from the optical axis normal to the slit plane.

\\lambda.name: Optical Wavelength
\\lambda.description: Wavelength of the incident monochromatic plane wave.

formulas.title: Circular-Aperture Airy Disk Intensity Pattern
formulas.description: Describes the radially symmetric far-field irradiance pattern $I(\theta)$ formed by a circular aperture of radius $a$ illuminated by plane waves of wavenumber $k = 2\pi/\lambda$, expressed in terms of the first-order Bessel function of the first kind $J_1$.
formulas.conceptual_definition: The Airy intensity distribution is the point-spread function of an ideal aberration-free circular lens or telescope mirror, replacing an ideal geometric point image with a finite bright disk surrounded by concentric rings.
formulas.intuitive_summary: Even a mathematically perfect telescope mirror cannot focus a distant star to a pinpoint; circular diffraction inevitably smears the image into a bullseye whose bright central Airy disk holds 83.8 percent of the light.
formulas.interpretation: Performing the two-dimensional Fraunhofer integral in polar coordinates yields the Hankel transform of a uniform disk, $2 J_1(u)/u$ with $u = k a \sin\theta = \pi D \sin\theta / \lambda$. The dark rings occur at the positive roots of $J_1(u) = 0$ ($u \approx 3.8317, 7.0156, 10.1735, \dots$), and the first bright ring peaks at just 1.75 percent of $I_0$.
formulas.symmetry_origin: Dictated by axial $SO(2)$ rotational invariance of a circular pupil, which converts the two-dimensional Cartesian Fourier transform into a zeroth-order Hankel transform evaluated via Bessel identities.
formulas.limits_and_boundary: As $u = k a \sin\theta \to 0$, $J_1(u) \approx u/2$ so $2J_1(u)/u \to 1$ and $I(0) = I_0$; for large $u$, the envelope decays as $u^{-3}$, faster than the $u^{-2}$ tail of a one-dimensional slit.

I(\\theta).name: Airy Pattern Irradiance
I(\\theta).description: Optical irradiance at polar diffraction angle $\theta$ from the optical axis.

J_1.name: First-Order Bessel Function of the First Kind
J_1.description: Cylindrical Bessel function $J_1(u)$ arising from integrating the circular aperture over radial and azimuthal coordinates.

a.name: Circular Aperture Radius
a.description: Radius of the circular pupil or objective lens ($a = D/2$).

\\theta.name: Polar Diffraction Angle
\\theta.description: Angular offset from the central optical axis.

formulas.title: Rayleigh Angular Resolution Criterion
formulas.description: Specifies the minimum resolvable angular separation $\theta_R$ between two equally bright incoherent point sources imaged through a circular aperture of diameter $D$ at wavelength $\lambda$, set by the first dark ring of the Airy disk.
formulas.conceptual_definition: The Rayleigh criterion defines the diffraction-limited angular resolution of a circular optical instrument by placing the central peak of one Airy pattern directly over the first zero of its neighbor.
formulas.intuitive_summary: To distinguish finer angular detail, an optical system must either collect light across a wider aperture $D$ or observe at a shorter wavelength $\lambda$.
formulas.interpretation: Setting the first zero of $J_1(\pi D \sin\theta / \lambda) = 0$ at $u_1 = 3.83170597$ gives $\sin\theta_R = (u_1 / \pi)(\lambda / D) \approx 1.21967 \lambda / D$. In the small-angle regime, the combined intensity of two equal incoherent sources separated by $\theta_R$ exhibits a 26.5 percent saddle dip between their peaks, cleanly signaling two distinct objects.
formulas.symmetry_origin: Directly inherits the $SO(2)$ circular pupil geometry of the Airy disk, with the numerical factor $1.21967 \approx 1.22$ fixed by the first positive root of $J_1(u)$ divided by $\pi$.
formulas.limits_and_boundary: Applies to aberration-free circular pupils in the small-angle paraxial regime ($\lambda \ll D$) for incoherent illumination; for high-NA microscopes, the analogous Abbe limit scales as $\lambda/(2\mathrm{NA})$, while coherent phase contrast or super-resolution fluorescence can surpass the classical Rayleigh dip.

\\theta_R.name: Rayleigh Minimum Resolvable Angle
\\theta_R.description: Minimum angular separation at which two incoherent point sources remain distinguishable under the Rayleigh criterion.

D.name: Circular Aperture Diameter
D.description: Full diameter of the limiting circular pupil, telescope mirror, or camera objective.

formulas.title: Diffraction Grating Equation and Chromatic Resolving Power
formulas.description: Combines the multi-slit diffraction grating condition $d(\sin\theta_m + \sin\theta_i) = m\lambda$ for constructive interference of order $m$ across groove spacing $d$ with the chromatic resolving power $R = \lambda / \Delta\lambda = m N$ achieved by illuminating $N$ coherent rulings.
formulas.conceptual_definition: A periodic array of $N$ identical apertures disperses wavelengths into discrete angular orders $m$ while sharpening spectral peaks inversely with $m N$ to enable high-resolution spectroscopy.
formulas.intuitive_summary: Light bounces or passes through thousands of evenly spaced grooves so that each color constructively reinforces at its own distinct angle; illuminating more grooves makes each spectral line razor-sharp.
formulas.interpretation: In the Fraunhofer regime, the $N$-slit interference factor $\sin^2(N\alpha)/\sin^2(\alpha)$ produces narrow principal maxima wherever the path difference $d(\sin\theta_m + \sin\theta_i)$ equals $m\lambda$. Applying the Rayleigh criterion—aligning the peak of $\lambda + \Delta\lambda$ with the first adjacent minimum of $\lambda$ at $\Delta(N\alpha) = \pi$—yields $R = \lambda / \Delta\lambda = m N$, which depends only on diffraction order and total illuminated groove count.
formulas.symmetry_origin: Arises from discrete one-dimensional translational symmetry of the grating lattice with period $d$, whose reciprocal lattice vectors $G_m = 2\pi m / d$ enforce conservation of transverse wavevector modulo $G_m$.
formulas.limits_and_boundary: For normal incidence ($\theta_i = 0$), the grating equation simplifies to $d\sin\theta_m = m\lambda$. Propagating orders exist only for $|m| \le 2d/\lambda$, and overlapping orders occur whenever $m_1 \lambda_1 = m_2 \lambda_2$; the total optical path difference $W = N d(\sin\theta_m + \sin\theta_i)$ bounds $R = W/\lambda$.

d.name: Grating Pitch
d.description: Center-to-center spacing between adjacent slits or ruled grooves.

\\theta_m.name: Diffracted Order Angle
\\theta_m.description: Angle of the $m$-th constructive interference maximum measured from the grating normal.

\\theta_i.name: Angle of Incidence
\\theta_i.description: Angle of the incoming collimated beam measured from the grating normal.

m.name: Diffraction Order
m.description: Integer index labeling the number of wavelengths of optical path difference between adjacent grooves.

\\lambda.name: Optical Wavelength
\\lambda.description: Wavelength of the dispersed monochromatic light.

R.name: Chromatic Resolving Power
R.description: Dimensionless spectral resolution $\lambda / \Delta\lambda$ quantifying the finest distinguishable wavelength separation.

\\Delta\\lambda.name: Minimum Resolvable Wavelength Difference
\\Delta\\lambda.description: Smallest wavelength interval separable under the Rayleigh criterion at wavelength $\lambda$.

N.name: Number of Illuminated Grooves
N.description: Total number of coherently illuminated periodic rulings across the diffraction grating.

formulas.title: First-Order Mutual Coherence Function
formulas.description: Defines the complex first-order mutual coherence function $\Gamma_{12}(\tau)$ as the stationary time-averaged cross-correlation between the complex analytic electric field $E(\mathbf{r}_1, t)$ at spacetime point $(\mathbf{r}_1, t)$ and $E(\mathbf{r}_2, t + \tau)$ at $(\mathbf{r}_2, t + \tau)$.
formulas.conceptual_definition: The mutual coherence function $\Gamma_{12}(\tau) = \langle E^*(\mathbf{r}_1, t) E(\mathbf{r}_2, t + \tau) \rangle$ quantifies the joint spatial and temporal correlation of an optical field between two points separated in space and delayed by time $\tau$.
formulas.intuitive_summary: It measures how reliably knowing the phase and amplitude of a light wave at one spot predicts the wave at a second spot a short moment later; high correlation produces crisp interference fringes.
formulas.interpretation: In any two-beam interference experiment combining fields from $(\mathbf{r}_1, t)$ and $(\mathbf{r}_2, t + \tau)$, the total time-averaged irradiance is $I = I_1 + I_2 + 2\,\mathrm{Re}[\Gamma_{12}(\tau)]$. Setting $\mathbf{r}_1 = \mathbf{r}_2$ and $\tau = 0$ recovers the local optical irradiance $\Gamma_{11}(0) = \langle |E(\mathbf{r}_1, t)|^2 \rangle$, while $\Gamma_{12}(\tau)$ itself obeys two coupled wave equations in vacuum.
formulas.symmetry_origin: Stationarity under time translation makes the correlation depend solely on the relative delay $\tau$ rather than absolute time $t$, and Hermitian conjugation enforces $\Gamma_{21}(-\tau) = \Gamma_{12}^*(\tau)$.
formulas.limits_and_boundary: For an ideal monochromatic plane wave, $|\Gamma_{12}(\tau)| = \sqrt{I_1 I_2}$ for all separations and delays; for thermal radiation in the limit $|\tau| \gg \tau_c$ or $|\mathbf{r}_2 - \mathbf{r}_1| \gg l_c$, $\Gamma_{12}(\tau) \to 0$ and interference vanishes.

\\Gamma_{12}(\\tau).name: Mutual Coherence Function
\\Gamma_{12}(\\tau).description: Complex cross-correlation function of the optical electric field between points $\mathbf{r}_1$ and $\mathbf{r}_2$ at relative time delay $\tau$.

E(\\mathbf{r}_2, t + \\tau).name: Complex Analytic Electric Field
E(\\mathbf{r}_2, t + \\tau).description: Positive-frequency complex representation of the scalar electric field evaluated at position $\mathbf{r}_2$ and delayed time $t + \tau$.

\\mathbf{r}_1.name: First Observation Position
\\mathbf{r}_1.description: Three-dimensional spatial coordinate of the first field sampling point or aperture.

\\mathbf{r}_2.name: Second Observation Position
\\mathbf{r}_2.description: Three-dimensional spatial coordinate of the second field sampling point or aperture.

\\tau.name: Relative Time Delay
\\tau.description: Temporal lag introduced between the two interfering optical paths.

formulas.title: Complex Degree of Coherence and Fringe Visibility
formulas.description: Relates the Michelson interference fringe visibility $V$ between maximum irradiance $I_{\max}$ and minimum irradiance $I_{\min}$ directly to the modulus of the normalized complex degree of coherence $|\gamma_{12}(\tau)|$ for equal-intensity interfering beams.
formulas.conceptual_definition: Fringe visibility $V = (I_{\max} - I_{\min})/(I_{\max} + I_{\min})$ measures the normalized contrast of an interference pattern and directly equals $|\gamma_{12}(\tau)|$ when both interfering arms carry equal optical power.
formulas.intuitive_summary: Visibility is the sharpness of bright and dark interference stripes: $V = 1$ means pitch-black dark fringes and perfect coherence, while $V = 0$ means uniform illumination with no fringes at all.
formulas.interpretation: For general beam irradiances $I_1$ and $I_2$, the fringe contrast obeys $V = \frac{2\sqrt{I_1 I_2}}{I_1 + I_2}|\gamma_{12}(\tau)|$. Matching the two arm intensities ($I_1 = I_2$) eliminates the geometric prefactor so that measuring fringe maxima and minima directly maps out $|\gamma_{12}(\tau)|$ as a function of delay or baseline.
formulas.symmetry_origin: Follows from the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality applied to the inner product $\langle E_1^* E_2 \rangle$, which bounds $|\gamma_{12}(\tau)| \in [0, 1]$ and guarantees non-negative optical irradiance $I_{\min} \ge 0$.
formulas.limits_and_boundary: At $|\gamma_{12}(\tau)| = 1$ (fully coherent equal beams), $I_{\min} = 0$ and $V = 1$; at $|\gamma_{12}(\tau)| = 0$ (incoherent beams), $I_{\max} = I_{\min} = I_1 + I_2$ and $V = 0$.

V.name: Fringe Visibility
V.description: Dimensionless Michelson contrast quantifying the relative modulation depth of interference fringes.

I_{\\max}.name: Maximum Fringe Irradiance
I_{\\max}.description: Peak time-averaged optical power per unit area at constructive interference.

I_{\\min}.name: Minimum Fringe Irradiance
I_{\\min}.description: Trough time-averaged optical power per unit area at destructive interference.

\\gamma_{12}(\\tau).name: Complex Degree of Coherence
\\gamma_{12}(\\tau).description: Normalized mutual coherence $\Gamma_{12}(\tau)/\sqrt{\Gamma_{11}(0)\Gamma_{22}(0)}$ whose magnitude lies between 0 and 1.

formulas.title: Temporal Coherence Length and Spectral Bandwidth
formulas.description: Expresses the longitudinal coherence length $L_c = c\tau_c$ of quasi-monochromatic light of center wavelength $\lambda$ and spectral linewidth $\Delta\lambda$, linking temporal correlation duration $\tau_c \sim 1/\Delta\nu$ to optical path difference limits.
formulas.conceptual_definition: The temporal coherence length $L_c = c\tau_c \approx \lambda^2/\Delta\lambda$ defines the maximum optical path-length difference over which a wave train remains phase-correlated with a delayed copy of itself.
formulas.intuitive_summary: Light with a narrower spread of colors stays in step with itself over a much longer distance; white light loses coherence after a few wavelengths, whereas a narrowband laser stays coherent for kilometers.
formulas.interpretation:
By the Wiener-Khinchin theorem, the temporal degree of coherence $\gamma(	au)$ is the Fourier transform of the normalized power spectrum $S(
u)$, enforcing the bandwidth-duration reciprocity $	au_c \Delta
u \sim 1$. Converting frequency spread $\Delta
u \approx (c/\lambda^2)\Delta\lambda$ yields $L_c = c	au_c \approx \lambda^2/\Delta\lambda$, with order-unity prefactors ($0.44$ for Gaussian spectra, $0.32$ for Lorentzian lines) depending on lineshape.
formulas.symmetry_origin: Emerges from the Fourier uncertainty relation between conjugate time delay $\tau$ and optical frequency $\nu$ under time-translation invariance of stationary random processes.
formulas.limits_and_boundary: As $\Delta\lambda \to 0$ (ideal monochromatic wave), $L_c \to \infty$; for broadband thermal light where $\Delta\lambda \sim \lambda$, $L_c$ collapses to a single optical wavelength, enabling micron-resolution optical coherence tomography.

L_c.name: Temporal Coherence Length
L_c.description: Longitudinal propagation distance over which the optical field maintains appreciable phase correlation.

c.name: Speed of Light in Vacuum
c.description: Universal propagation speed of electromagnetic waves in vacuum.

\\tau_c.name: Coherence Time
\\tau_c.description: Characteristic decay time of the temporal autocorrelation function $|\gamma(\tau)|$.

\\lambda.name: Center Wavelength
\\lambda.description: Mean vacuum wavelength of the optical radiation.

\\Delta\\lambda.name: Spectral Bandwidth
\\Delta\\lambda.description: Full width at half maximum of the optical power spectrum in wavelength units.

formulas.title: van Cittert-Zernike Spatial Coherence Theorem
formulas.equation: \gamma_{12}(0) = \frac{\iint I(\boldsymbol{\theta}) e^{-i k \boldsymbol{\theta} \cdot \Delta\mathbf{r}} \, d^2\theta}{\iint I(\boldsymbol{\theta}) \, d^2\theta}
formulas.description: States that the equal-time complex degree of spatial coherence $\gamma_{12}(0)$ across transverse baseline $\Delta\mathbf{r}$ in the far field of a spatially incoherent quasi-monochromatic source equals the normalized two-dimensional Fourier transform of the source angular intensity profile $I(\boldsymbol{\theta})$.
formulas.conceptual_definition: The van Cittert-Zernike theorem connects the spatial coherence measured between two distant receivers to the Fourier transform of an incoherent emitter's brightness distribution on the sky.
formulas.intuitive_summary: Even a completely jumbled thermal source like a star produces correlated ripples at distant telescopes, and the fringe contrast measured across different telescope baselines maps out the star's angular size and shape.
formulas.interpretation: In the paraxial far-field regime, each incoherent source element at angular coordinate $\boldsymbol{\theta}$ radiates a spherical wave contributing a phase factor $e^{-i k \boldsymbol{\theta} \cdot \Delta\mathbf{r}}$ across baseline $\Delta\mathbf{r}$. Measuring $|\gamma_{12}(0)|$ across multiple baselines therefore reconstructs stellar angular diameters (via Michelson stellar interferometry) and aperture-synthesis images in optical and radio astronomy.
formulas.symmetry_origin: Follows from Fresnel-Fraunhofer Huygens propagation of spatially delta-correlated source fields under transverse shift invariance in the paraxial far field.
formulas.limits_and_boundary: As baseline $|\Delta\mathbf{r}| \to 0$, $\gamma_{12}(0) \to 1$; for a uniform circular disk of angular diameter $\theta_s$, $\gamma_{12}(0) = 2 J_1(\pi \theta_s d / \lambda)/(\pi \theta_s d / \lambda)$, vanishing first at $d = 1.22\lambda/\theta_s$.

\\gamma_{12}(0).name: Equal-Time Spatial Degree of Coherence
\\gamma_{12}(0).description: Normalized complex spatial coherence between two observation points separated by baseline $\Delta\mathbf{r}$ at zero time delay.

I(\\boldsymbol{\\theta}).name: Source Angular Intensity Distribution
I(\\boldsymbol{\\theta}).description: Radiance or surface brightness of the incoherent extended source as a function of two-dimensional sky angle $\boldsymbol{\theta}$.

k.name: Optical Wavenumber
k.description: Spatial angular frequency $k = 2\pi/\lambda$ of the quasi-monochromatic radiation.

\\boldsymbol{\\theta}.name: Angular Source Coordinate
\\boldsymbol{\\theta}.description: Two-dimensional angular position vector across the emitting surface of the distant source.

\\Delta\\mathbf{r}.name: Interferometer Baseline Vector
\\Delta\\mathbf{r}.description: Transverse spatial separation vector $\mathbf{r}_2 - \mathbf{r}_1$ between the two receiving apertures.

formulas.title: Fabry-Pérot Airy Transmission Function
formulas.description: Gives the steady-state intensity transmittance $T(\delta)$ of a lossless parallel-plate Fabry-Pérot optical resonator as a function of round-trip phase shift $\delta = (4\pi n L \cos\theta)/\lambda$ and coefficient of finesse $F$.
formulas.conceptual_definition: The Airy transmission function $T(\delta) = [1 + F\sin^2(\delta/2)]^{-1}$ describes the sharp periodic resonant transmission peaks arising from infinite multiple-beam interference inside a two-mirror optical cavity.
formulas.intuitive_summary: Two highly reflective mirrors facing each other block almost all light except at exact resonant wavelengths where internal reflections add up in phase, letting 100 percent of the resonant beam pass cleanly through.
formulas.interpretation: Summing the transmitted electric-field geometric series $E_t = E_0 (1 - R) \sum_{m=0}^{\infty} (R e^{i\delta})^m = E_0 (1 - R)/(1 - R e^{i\delta})$ and taking $|E_t/E_0|^2$ yields the Airy formula with $F = 4R/(1 - R)^2$. Near any resonance $\delta = 2\pi m + \epsilon$ with $|\epsilon| \ll 1$, $\sin(\delta/2) \approx \epsilon/2$ and the transmission peak reduces to a Lorentzian lineshape.
formulas.symmetry_origin: Follows from energy conservation ($T + R_{\mathrm{cav}} = 1$ for lossless mirrors) and discrete translational periodicity under $\delta \to \delta + 2\pi$.
formulas.limits_and_boundary: At resonance ($\delta = 2\pi m$), $T = 1$ identically regardless of how close $R$ is to unity; midway between resonances ($\delta = (2m+1)\pi$), $T_{\min} = (1 + F)^{-1} = [(1-R)/(1+R)]^2$, which vanishes rapidly as $R \to 1$.

T(\\delta).name: Cavity Intensity Transmittance
T(\\delta).description: Ratio of transmitted to incident optical irradiance through the Fabry-Pérot resonator.

\\delta.name: Round-Trip Optical Phase Shift
\\delta.description: Phase difference $4\pi n L \cos\theta / \lambda$ accumulated between successive transmitted partial waves.

F.name: Coefficient of Finesse
F.description: Dimensionless mirror-reflectivity parameter $4R/(1 - R)^2$ governing fringe contrast and sharpness.

formulas.title: Fabry-Pérot Cavity Finesse and Coefficient of Finesse
formulas.description: Defines the reflectivity-limited cavity finesse $\mathcal{F}$—the ratio of free spectral range to resonance linewidth—and the coefficient of finesse $F$ in terms of mirror intensity reflectivity $R$.
formulas.conceptual_definition: Cavity finesse $\mathcal{F} \approx \pi\sqrt{R}/(1 - R)$ measures the sharpness of Fabry-Pérot transmission peaks relative to their spacing and scales directly with the average number of round trips a photon makes before escaping.
formulas.intuitive_summary: The closer mirror reflectivity $R$ gets to 100 percent, the more times light bounces inside the cavity, making the resonant transmission spikes dramatically narrower and boosting phase sensitivity.
formulas.interpretation: Setting $T(\delta) = 1/2$ in the Airy function gives the half-maximum phase width $\delta_{\mathrm{FWHM}} = 4 \arcsin(1/\sqrt{F})$. For high reflectivity ($F \gg 1$), $\delta_{\mathrm{FWHM}} \approx 4/\sqrt{F} = 2(1 - R)/\sqrt{R}$, so $\mathcal{F} = 2\pi/\delta_{\mathrm{FWHM}} \approx \pi\sqrt{R}/(1 - R)$. In ultrastable optical-clock cavities with $1 - R \sim 10^{-5}$, $\mathcal{F}$ exceeds $10^5$.
formulas.symmetry_origin: Reflects the dimensionless scaling of cavity resonance selectivity with mirror loss $1 - R$ under multiple-beam coherent summation.

formulas.conceptual_definition: The free spectral range $\Delta\nu_{\mathrm{FSR}} = c/(2 n L)$ is the inverse round-trip transit time of light inside a linear resonator, setting the uniform frequency spacing between adjacent longitudinal transmission peaks.
formulas.intuitive_summary: A Fabry-Pérot cavity acts like a frequency comb whose resonant teeth repeat every $c/(2 n L)$; shorter cavities space their resonances wide apart, while kilometer-long cavities pack them closely together.

u)^{-1}$.

formulas.title: Fermat's Variational Principle of Stationary Optical Path
formulas.description: States that the actual path traversed by a light ray between fixed endpoints $A$ and $B$ makes the first variation of the optical path length $\int_A^B n(\mathbf{r})\,ds$ vanish.
formulas.conceptual_definition: Fermat's principle $\delta \int_A^B n(\mathbf{r})\,ds = 0$ is the variational foundation of geometric optics, asserting that physical light rays follow stationary-time (geodesic) paths in the refractive-index metric.
formulas.intuitive_summary: Among all conceivable routes between two points, light chooses a path whose travel time does not change to first order when the route is wiggled slightly—often the fastest path, and occasionally a local maximum or saddle point.
formulas.interpretation: In terms of vacuum light speed $c$, travel time is $T = (1/c)\int_A^B n\,ds$. Constructive interference in the Feynman path-integral or Huygens-Fresnel superposition selects paths of stationary phase $k_0 \int n\,ds$, explaining why Fermat's principle holds in the short-wavelength limit and mirrors Maupertuis's principle $\delta \int p\,ds = 0$ in classical mechanics.
formulas.symmetry_origin: Expresses reparameterization invariance of the optical geodesic functional and reflects the stationary-phase limit of electromagnetic wave superposition.
formulas.limits_and_boundary: Valid when path-length differences across neighboring trajectories vary rapidly compared to $\lambda_0$; fails at caustics and foci where second variations vanish and diffraction governs field amplitudes.

formulas.title: Paraxial ABCD Ray Transfer Matrix and Symplectic Invariant
formulas.equation: \begin{pmatrix} y_2 \\ \theta_2 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} A & B \\ C & D \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} y_1 \\ \theta_1 \end{pmatrix}, \quad AD - BC = \frac{n_1}{n_2}
formulas.description: Linearly transforms a paraxial ray's transverse height $y_1$ and slope angle $\theta_1$ at an input plane in medium $n_1$ to $(y_2, \theta_2)^T$ at an output plane in medium $n_2$ via a $2\times 2$ system matrix obeying the determinant constraint $AD - BC = n_1/n_2$.
formulas.conceptual_definition: The ABCD ray transfer matrix formalism represents every paraxial optical element—free-space drifts, curved refracting surfaces, mirrors, and lenses—as a linear $2\times 2$ symplectic map whose determinant enforces conservation of optical étendue.
formulas.intuitive_summary: For rays staying close to the optical axis, passing through an entire telescope or laser cavity reduces to multiplying simple $2\times 2$ matrices, with the determinant fixed by the ratio of entrance and exit refractive indices.
formulas.interpretation: In canonical optical phase space $(y, p_y)$ with reduced slope $p_y = n\theta$, the transfer matrix belongs to the symplectic group $\mathrm{Sp}(2,\mathbb{R})$ with unit determinant, immediately yielding $AD - BC = n_1/n_2$ in $(y, \theta)$ coordinates. Special matrix zeros have direct physical meaning: $B = 0$ specifies imaging planes, $C = 0$ defines afocal telescopic systems, and $A = 0$ or $D = 0$ locates focal planes.
formulas.symmetry_origin: Follows from Hamiltonian symplecticity of Fermat's variational principle linearized around a straight optical axis with axial rotational symmetry.
formulas.limits_and_boundary: Strictly accurate in the first-order paraxial regime ($|\theta| \ll 1$, $\sin\theta \approx \theta$); higher-order terms in $\theta^3$ generate the five primary Seidel aberrations.

formulas.title: Gaussian Thin-Lens and Lensmaker Equation
formulas.description: Relates object distance $s_o$, image distance $s_i$, and focal length $f$ for a thin spherical lens in air of refractive index $n$ and surface radii of curvature $R_1$ and $R_2$.
formulas.conceptual_definition: The thin-lens and lensmaker equation determines both the optical power $1/f$ of a negligible-thickness refractive lens from its geometry and index and the conjugate object-image plane locations where paraxial rays converge.
formulas.intuitive_summary: A curved piece of glass bends parallel light to a focal point determined by its refractive index and surface curvatures, and maps any object plane to a sharp conjugate image plane obeying the reciprocal sum $1/s_o + 1/s_i = 1/f$.
formulas.interpretation: Multiplying two spherical refraction matrices separated by zero thickness yields the thin-lens matrix with $A = D = 1$, $B = 0$, and $C = -1/f = -(n-1)(1/R_1 - 1/R_2)$. Cascading drifts $s_o$ and $s_i$ gives total element $B_{\mathrm{tot}} = s_o + s_i - s_o s_i / f$; setting $B_{\mathrm{tot}} = 0$ for point-to-point imaging yields $1/s_o + 1/s_i = 1/f$ with lateral magnification $M = -s_i/s_o$.
formulas.symmetry_origin: Inherits time-reversal reciprocity of optical paths, making the object and image distances $s_o$ and $s_i$ symmetrically interchangeable.
formulas.limits_and_boundary: Valid when lens center thickness $d \ll |R_1|, |R_2|, |f|$ and rays remain paraxial; for an object at infinity ($s_o \to \infty$), the image forms at the back focal plane $s_i = f$.

formulas.title: Two-Mirror Optical Resonator Stability Criterion
formulas.description: Specifies the geometric confinement condition for a two-mirror optical cavity of length $L$ and mirror radii of curvature $R_1, R_2$ to trap paraxial rays and support bounded Gaussian eigenmodes over arbitrary round trips.
formulas.conceptual_definition: The resonator stability inequality $0 \le g_1 g_2 \le 1$ partitions all two-mirror laser cavity geometries into stable trapping regions where rays oscillate periodically and unstable regions where rays walk exponentially off the axis.
formulas.intuitive_summary: A laser cavity traps light between two curved mirrors only when the mirror curvatures and spacing keep rays periodically refocused rather than walking off the mirror edges after a few bounces.
formulas.interpretation: For a round trip through cavity length $L$ and mirrors of focal lengths $f_i = R_i/2$, the unimodular round-trip matrix has half-trace $(A+D)/2 = 2 g_1 g_2 - 1$. Requiring $|A+D|/2 \le 1$ so the eigenvalues $e^{\pm i\phi}$ remain on the unit circle gives $-1 \le 2g_1 g_2 - 1 \le 1$, or $0 \le g_1 g_2 \le 1$.
formulas.symmetry_origin: Stems from spectral stability of unimodular $\mathrm{SL}(2,\mathbb{R})$ matrices whose complex-conjugate eigenvalues preserve symplectic phase-space ellipses.
formulas.limits_and_boundary: The boundary $g_1 g_2 = 1$ includes planar ($R_1 = R_2 = \infty$) and concentric ($R_1 = R_2 = L/2$) cavities; $g_1 g_2 = 0$ corresponds to symmetric confocal ($R_1 = R_2 = L$) and hemispherical resonators; $g_1 g_2 < 0$ or $> 1$ defines unstable resonators.

formulas.title: Kogelnik ABCD Law for Gaussian Beam Propagation
formulas.equation: q_2 = \frac{A q_1 + B}{C q_1 + D}, \quad \frac{1}{q(z)} = \frac{1}{R(z)} - \frac{i \lambda}{\pi n w^2(z)}
formulas.description: Transforms the complex Gaussian beam parameter $q(z) = z + i z_R$ through any paraxial optical system via a Möbius fractional linear transformation governed by the system's geometric ABCD ray matrix.
formulas.conceptual_definition: Kogelnik's ABCD law unifies geometric ray matrices with paraxial wave diffraction by encoding both wavefront curvature $R(z)$ and beam spot radius $w(z)$ inside a single complex parameter $q(z)$ that transforms bilinearly under every paraxial optical element.
formulas.intuitive_summary: The exact same $2\times 2$ ray matrix that tracks straight geometric rays also predicts how a real diffracting Gaussian laser beam focuses, expands, and curves through lenses and laser cavities.
formulas.interpretation: In free space ($A=D=1, B=z, C=0$), $q(z) = q_0 + z = z + i z_R$ with Rayleigh range $z_R = \pi n w_0^2 / \lambda$, immediately yielding hyperbolic waist expansion $w(z) = w_0\sqrt{1 + (z/z_R)^2}$ and curvature $R(z) = z[1 + (z_R/z)^2]$. Passing through a thin lens ($A=D=1, B=0, C=-1/f$) shifts $1/q_2 = 1/q_1 - 1/f$, curving the wavefront while preserving spot size at the lens plane.
formulas.symmetry_origin: Reflects the projective Möbius action of the symplectic group $\mathrm{SL}(2,\mathbb{R})$ on the upper half of the complex $q$-plane, preserving $\mathrm{Im}(q) > 0$.
formulas.limits_and_boundary: In the geometric-optics limit $\lambda \to 0$, $1/q(z) \to 1/R(z)$ and the law reduces to the spherical-wavefront radius transformation; breaks down for non-paraxial tightly focused beams with numerical aperture approaching unity.

formulas.title: Angular Spectrum Free-Space Transfer Function
formulas.equation: H(f_x, f_y; z) = \exp\!\left[ i k z \sqrt{1 - (\lambda f_x)^2 - (\lambda f_y)^2} \right]
formulas.description: Exact linear shift-invariant transfer function $H(f_x, f_y; z)$ propagating the two-dimensional angular spectrum of a monochromatic optical field of wavelength $\lambda$ and wavenumber $k = 2\pi/\lambda$ across a homogeneous free-space distance $z$.
formulas.conceptual_definition: The angular spectrum transfer function multiplies each plane-wave Fourier component $(f_x, f_y)$ by its exact axial propagation factor $\exp(i k_z z)$ determined by the scalar Helmholtz dispersion relation.
formulas.intuitive_summary: Free space acts like a spatial-frequency filter: waves tilted at real angles simply shift in phase as they travel forward, while ripples finer than one wavelength die away exponentially before reaching the far field.
formulas.interpretation: Substituting a plane-wave Fourier decomposition into the three-dimensional Helmholtz equation $(\nabla^2 + k^2)U = 0$ yields $d^2 A/dz^2 + k_z^2 A = 0$ with $k_z = k\sqrt{1 - (\lambda f_x)^2 - (\lambda f_y)^2}$. Inside the propagating circle $f_x^2 + f_y^2 \le 1/\lambda^2$, $|H| = 1$ and energy propagates without loss; outside it ($f_x^2 + f_y^2 > 1/\lambda^2$), $k_z$ becomes purely imaginary and $|H| = \exp(-|k_z| z)$ exponentially damps evanescent sub-wavelength features.
formulas.symmetry_origin: Follows directly from transverse Euclidean translation invariance of homogeneous space, which diagonalizes the three-dimensional Helmholtz operator in the two-dimensional plane-wave Fourier basis.
formulas.limits_and_boundary: At $z = 0$, $H = 1$ identically. In the paraxial limit $(\lambda f_x)^2 + (\lambda f_y)^2 \ll 1$, expanding the square root to first order recovers the Fresnel quadratic phase transfer function. For $z \gg \lambda$, evanescent modes with $f_x^2 + f_y^2 > 1/\lambda^2$ vanish completely.

formulas.title: Paraxial Fresnel Free-Space Transfer Function
formulas.equation: H_{\mathrm{F}}(f_x, f_y; z) = e^{i k z} \exp\!\left[ -i \pi \lambda z \left( f_x^2 + f_y^2 \right) \right]
formulas.description: Paraxial (Fresnel) approximation to the free-space transfer function $H_{\mathrm{F}}(f_x, f_y; z)$, obtained by expanding the exact angular-spectrum square root to quadratic order in $\lambda f_x$ and $\lambda f_y$.
formulas.conceptual_definition: In the paraxial regime where waves travel close to the optical axis, free-space diffraction acts as an all-pass quadratic phase chirp in spatial-frequency space.
formulas.intuitive_summary: For shallow-angle beams, each spatial frequency accumulates a phase lag proportional to the square of its tilt angle and the propagation distance, just like a quantum wavepacket spreading in time.
formulas.interpretation: Approximating $\sqrt{1 - (\lambda f_x)^2 - (\lambda f_y)^2} \approx 1 - \frac{1}{2}[(\lambda f_x)^2 + (\lambda f_y)^2]$ and using $k\lambda = 2\pi$ converts the exact transfer function into $e^{ikz}\exp[-i\pi\lambda z(f_x^2 + f_y^2)]$. Inverse Fourier transformation yields the Fresnel convolution kernel, making paraxial optics mathematically isomorphic to the free-particle two-dimensional Schrödinger equation with $z$ playing the role of time.
formulas.symmetry_origin: Reflects the Galilean-like paraxial symmetry of the slowly varying envelope equation $2ik\,\partial_z A + \nabla_\perp^2 A = 0$ under small-angle beam tilts.
formulas.limits_and_boundary: Accurate whenever $(\lambda f_x)^2 + (\lambda f_y)^2 \ll 1$ and higher-order quartic phase errors $\frac{1}{8} k z \lambda^4 (f_x^2 + f_y^2)^2 \ll 1$. Breaks down for high-numerical-aperture focusing or sub-wavelength near fields.

formulas.title: Thin-Lens Quadratic Phase Transmittance
formulas.description: Complex amplitude transmittance $t_l(x, y)$ of an ideal paraxial thin lens of focal length $f$, omitting the constant axial phase offset and finite pupil aperture.
formulas.conceptual_definition: A thin converging lens bends a flat incident wavefront into a converging spherical wave by imposing a radially quadratic phase advance relative to its thicker center.
formulas.intuitive_summary: Because glass slows light down and a converging lens is thickest at the center and thinner at the rim, outer rays pull ahead quadratically in phase, curving a flat wavefront toward the focal point.
formulas.interpretation: In the thin-lens approximation where a ray exits at the same transverse coordinates $(x, y)$ at which it entered, the optical path length through spherical surfaces of radii $R_1$ and $R_2$ varies as $-(x^2 + y^2)/(2f)$ with $1/f = (n - 1)(1/R_1 - 1/R_2)$. For $f > 0$ (converging lens), the negative quadratic phase transforms an incident plane wave into a paraxial spherical wave converging to $z = f$; for $f < 0$, it produces a diverging spherical wave.
formulas.symmetry_origin: Governed by rotational symmetry about the optical axis and the paraxial spherical-surface approximation $z(r) \approx r^2 / (2R)$.
formulas.limits_and_boundary: Valid when the lens thickness is negligible compared to $f$ and ray heights satisfy $x^2 + y^2 \ll f^2$. Larger apertures introduce fourth-order spherical aberration terms proportional to $(x^2 + y^2)^2$.

formulas.title: Back Focal Plane Optical Fourier Transform
formulas.equation: U_f(x_f, y_f) = \frac{1}{i \lambda f} \iint_{-\infty}^{\infty} U_0(x_0, y_0) \exp\!\left[ -i \frac{2\pi}{\lambda f} (x_f x_0 + y_f y_0) \right] dx_0 \, dy_0
formulas.description: Exact two-dimensional Fourier transform relation mapping an input field $U_0(x_0, y_0)$ in the front focal plane of a thin lens of focal length $f$ to the complex field $U_f(x_f, y_f)$ in its back focal plane.
formulas.conceptual_definition: A converging lens focuses every parallel bundle of diffracted rays to a unique point $(x_f, y_f) = (\lambda f f_x, \lambda f f_y)$ in its back focal plane, physically computing a two-dimensional Fourier transform without residual phase curvature.
formulas.intuitive_summary: Place an illuminated pattern one focal length in front of a lens, and the light pattern one focal length behind the lens is literally its exact two-dimensional spatial-frequency spectrum.
formulas.interpretation: Combining Fresnel propagation over distance $f$ from the object to the lens, multiplication by the quadratic lens phase $\exp[-i k (x^2 + y^2)/(2f)]$, and Fresnel propagation over distance $f$ to the back focal plane cancels the outer quadratic phase factor identically. This exact transform underlies Abbe's theory of image formation and enables direct spatial filtering in the central plane of a $4f$ optical correlator.
formulas.symmetry_origin: Arises from exact cancellation between the quadratic Fresnel diffraction chirp and the conjugate quadratic phase transmittance of a thin lens in the symmetric $2f$ geometry.
formulas.limits_and_boundary: Holds strictly in the paraxial limit when the lens pupil aperture is much larger than the illuminated object and diffracted beam spread; finite lens apertures introduce vignetting that attenuates high spatial frequencies.

formulas.title: Zernike Phase-Contrast Image Intensity
formulas.description: Linearized image-plane irradiance $I_{\mathrm{Z}}(x, y)$ produced by a Zernike phase-contrast microscope when a weak phase object $t(x, y) \approx 1 + i\phi(x, y)$ has its undiffracted DC Fourier order phase-shifted by $+\pi/2$.
formulas.conceptual_definition: Shifting the central zero-frequency order by $\pi/2$ in the back focal plane rotates the background wave into phase with the scattered wave, transforming invisible phase variations $\phi(x, y)$ linearly into visible brightness contrast.
formulas.intuitive_summary: A transparent living cell barely absorbs light, so it looks invisible under a normal microscope; shifting just the unscattered background beam by a quarter-wave makes thicker parts of the cell shine brightly or darken proportionally to their phase shift.
formulas.interpretation: Without a phase plate, $|1 + i\phi|^2 = 1 + \phi^2 \approx 1$ has no first-order sensitivity to $\phi(x, y)$. Inserting a quarter-wave dot at the $4f$ Fourier origin multiplies the DC term $1$ by $i$ (positive phase contrast) or $-i$ (negative phase contrast), yielding an image field $U_{\mathrm{Z}} \approx i[1 + \phi(x, y)]$ whose squared modulus $I_{\mathrm{Z}} = I_0(1 + 2\phi + \phi^2) \approx I_0(1 + 2\phi)$ renders phase shifts directly visible.
formulas.symmetry_origin: Exploits the $\pi/2$ quadrature phase symmetry between the zeroth-order background and first-order scattered wave of any lossless unitary phase transmittance $|t(x, y)| = 1$.
formulas.limits_and_boundary: Valid in the weak-phase regime $|\phi(x, y)| \ll 1$. For large phase steps ($|\phi| \gtrsim 1\,\mathrm{rad}$), the linear relation saturates and finite phase-ring widths produce characteristic bright halos around sharp specimen edges.

I_{\\mathrm{Z}}.name: Phase-Contrast Image Irradiance
I_{\\mathrm{Z}}.description: Measured optical intensity across the image plane after DC phase shifting.

I_0.description: Uniform incident intensity in the absence of phase variations.

formulas.title: Optical Transfer Function Pupil Autocorrelation
formulas.equation: \mathcal{H}(f_x, f_y) = \frac{\iint P(\xi, \eta) P^*(\xi - \lambda d_i f_x, \eta - \lambda d_i f_y) \, d\xi \, d\eta}{\iint |P(\xi, \eta)|^2 \, d\xi \, d\eta}
formulas.description: Normalized incoherent optical transfer function $\mathcal{H}(f_x, f_y)$ expressed as the two-dimensional autocorrelation of the generalized exit-pupil function $P(\xi, \eta)$ scaled by $\lambda d_i$.
formulas.conceptual_definition: Because the incoherent point-spread function is the squared modulus of the coherent impulse response, the convolution theorem forces the incoherent optical transfer function to equal the normalized autocorrelation of the coherent pupil function.
formulas.intuitive_summary: For incoherent light, how well a lens transmits a striped pattern equals the overlapping area of the lens pupil with a shifted copy of itself—reaching zero once the two copies no longer overlap at twice the coherent cutoff frequency.
formulas.interpretation: In an aberration-free circular pupil of diameter $D$, the overlap of two shifted circles decays monotonically from $1$ at $(f_x, f_y) = (0, 0)$ to $0$ at the incoherent cutoff frequency $f_c = D / (\lambda d_i) = 2\mathrm{NA}/\lambda$. Wavefront aberrations enter as a complex phase factor $\exp[i k W(\xi, \eta)]$ inside $P(\xi, \eta)$; by the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality, phase variations across the overlap region can only reduce the modulation transfer function $\mathrm{MTF} = |\mathcal{H}|$ relative to the diffraction-limited ideal.
formulas.symmetry_origin: Follows directly from the Wiener-Khinchin and Fourier autocorrelation theorems applied to the real, non-negative incoherent point-spread function $|h(x, y)|^2$, guaranteeing Hermitian symmetry $\mathcal{H}(-f_x, -f_y) = \mathcal{H}^*(f_x, f_y)$.
formulas.limits_and_boundary: Normalized so $\mathcal{H}(0, 0) = 1$ and $|\mathcal{H}(f_x, f_y)| \le 1$ everywhere. Vanishes identically for $\sqrt{f_x^2 + f_y^2} \ge 2\mathrm{NA}/\lambda$ in a circularly symmetric system.

formulas.title: Off-Axis Hologram Interference Intensity
formulas.description: Recorded interference irradiance $I_h(x, y) = |R + O|^2$ formed by superposing a coherent reference beam $R(x, y)$ with a scattered object wavefront $O(x, y)$ across a holographic recording medium.
formulas.conceptual_definition: Interfering an unknown complex object wave with a known coherent reference wave encodes both the object's amplitude and phase into intensity fringes via the twin cross-terms $R^* O$ and $R O^*$.
formulas.intuitive_summary: A camera alone forgets the timing of light waves, flattening a 3D scene; mixing in a tilted reference laser beam turns wave phase into fine zebra-like fringes so shining the reference beam back through the recording rebuilds the full 3D wavefront.
formulas.interpretation: In off-axis Leith-Upatnieks holography, $R(x, y) = R_0 \exp(i 2\pi f_0 x)$ carries a spatial carrier frequency $f_0$ exceeding three times the object bandwidth $B_O$. In spatial-frequency space, the zero-order DC background $|R|^2 + |O|^2$ sits centered at the origin, while the virtual-image term $R^* O$ and conjugate real-image term $R O^*$ shift to $\mp f_0$, preventing twin-image overlap during optical or digital reconstruction.
formulas.symmetry_origin: Follows directly from the bilinear superposition principle of coherent electromagnetic fields and the square-law intensity response of optical detectors.
formulas.limits_and_boundary: Clean spatial separation of the reconstructed twin images requires an off-axis carrier frequency satisfying $f_0 \ge 3 B_O$ (or $f_0 \ge B_O$ when $|R| \gg |O|$ so $|O|^2$ is negligible); when $f_0 = 0$, the equation reduces to Gabor's inline hologram where twin images overlap along the optical axis.

I_h.name: Hologram Interference Irradiance
I_h.description: Total time-averaged optical intensity recorded across the hologram plane $(x, y)$.

R.name: Coherent Reference Wave Amplitude
R.description: Complex scalar field amplitude (in irradiance-normalized units) of the tilted coherent reference beam.

O.name: Object Wavefront Complex Amplitude
O.description: Complex scalar field amplitude scattered from the three-dimensional object onto the recording plane.
